docs.title: Purgatorium (p9m)
docs.text:
Early, before 1.0

It works and is tested (CI on every change, releases with a changelog), but expect rough edges, and breaking changes between minor versions.

Self-hosted sandboxes for your team and their AI agents: everyone gets their own Docker, every app gets a URL, idle sandboxes sleep.

About 10 seconds from New sandbox to your own Docker and a public URL for your app; a sleeping sandbox is back in under 10. (Measured with the images already pulled: the first sandbox on a new server also downloads them.)

The same from a script or an agent, all real runs:

With curl, through the API By an agent, over the MCP server The MCP server by hand (JSON-RPC)

Where your team's code waits before it goes to heaven (production). Nothing is lost here: idle sandboxes sleep, deleted ones are archived. p9m is the short name, as in k8s: purgatory, 7 letters in between. It names the sandboxes (p9m-<name>), labels, tokens and the UI address.

Purgatorium gives each user their own Docker daemon on demand — not a shared platform where you deploy apps, but a full Docker engine they own, with a public URL for every app (and a Portainer UI if they want one), provisioned in seconds from the web UI or a REST API.

Just want your app online?

Tutorials: with Claude Code, install the p9m plugin once and say deploy this app; you get a link that works for anyone.

docs.title: Who is this for
docs.text: Teams where people need to spin up arbitrary Docker workloads without touching shared infrastructure. Designed for vibe-coded apps: your colleague runs an AI agent, gets a docker-compose.yml, and the agent deploys it into their sandbox (or they paste it into Portainer), done.

docs.title: What each sandbox gets
docs.text:
• Its own Docker daemon (Docker-in-Docker; see Security for what that does and does not isolate)
  • Access for agents and people — the docker command line straight to the sandbox's daemon, SSH, a browser terminal, an MCP server; a token limited to the sandbox is enough for an agent to deploy, build and update (agent guide)
  • Portainer UI if you want one — the portainer template adds it, with generated credentials
  • FRP tunnel — public URLs for services running inside the sandbox
  • Sleeps when idle — after idle_timeout without HTTP traffic the sandbox is stopped; the next request wakes it (Sablier)
  • Nothing is ever destroyed automatically — an explicit delete archives the sandbox (config + data) instead of discarding it
  • Template-based — define what goes into a sandbox via YAML

docs.title: Why Purgatorium
docs.text:
A self-hosted Vercel or Railway for the whole team: everyone gets their own Docker, every app a URL, and idle apps cost nothing.

Purgatorium Cloud PaaS (Vercel, Railway, Render, Fly.io) Shared VPS / Coolify / Dokploy Runs on your own server, one docker compose their cloud your own server You pay for the server every project and its usage the server Each person gets their own Docker daemon, any compose stack projects on a team account projects on a shared daemon Public URL for every app automatic automatic Coolify / Dokploy: automatic Idle sleeps, wakes on the next request runs and is billed, or scales to zero on some keeps running On delete archives deletes deletes

In short: pick Purgatorium for the many apps a team builds before production (experiments, demos, internal tools, vibe-coded apps), on your own hardware. For production that must scale, pick a cloud PaaS or Coolify / Dokploy; for untrusted code, a microVM. Coder or Codespaces are for writing code, E2B or Daytona for an agent's short runs: different jobs. The full comparison: docs/comparison.md.

Next: install it, then create your first sandbox.

docs.title: Purgatorium for agents: deploy and update apps in a sandbox
docs.text:
This guide is for a coding agent (for example Claude Code on the user's machine) that deploys or updates apps in the user's Purgatorium sandbox. Every call below was run against a live Purgatorium.

Every sandbox has its own Docker daemon. The agent works with:

  • the Purgatorium API, with the user's personal access token, to find the sandbox, wake it and get its Docker client certificates;
  • the sandbox's Docker daemon, with the plain docker command line, to deploy, build and update.

An agent with MCP can make the Purgatorium API calls as tools instead: see MCP. A sandbox made from the portainer template also has a Portainer API: see With Portainer at the end.

docs.title: What the user gives the agent
docs.text:
Value Example Where it comes from Purgatorium URL https://p9m.example.com The address of the Purgatorium UI Personal access token p9m_… UI → My area → Access tokens → + New token Sandbox name p9m-shop The name in the UI list with the p9m- prefix

The user may instead give these in a p9m.env file in the project (UI → the new token → Download p9m.env; it may also be renamed .env or copied into one): P9M_URL, P9M_TOKEN, P9M_SANDBOX (only for a token limited to one sandbox; otherwise ask which sandbox, or list them with GET /sandboxes) and P9M_AGENT_GUIDE (this guide). Read them from there; do not print the token or commit the file.

The token may be limited to one sandbox. Then GET /sandboxes lists only that one, GET /me returns it as sandbox, and creating or deleting sandboxes answers 403. Everything in this guide works with such a token.

Every Purgatorium API call sends Authorization: Bearer p9m_…. The token acts as the user: it sees and changes only the user's own sandboxes.

docs.title: 1. Find the sandbox and wake it
docs.text:
GET /sandboxes/p9m-shop

The answer includes:

  • status: running, exited (asleep) or deep_sleep;
  • docker_access: host, the address of the sandbox's Docker daemon (for example shop-docker.example.com), and state: ready, or needs-certs when its certificates do not cover that address (the user enables it once: Access → Enable, which restarts the sandbox); and, while the sandbox is not running, hint: a Docker connection does not wake it, so start it first (docker would only get EOF);
  • with ?include_keys=true only: ca_cert, client_cert, client_key, the Docker client certificates and private key (PEM). Write them to files with a program (below), never by copying them through a model: copied by hand a key gets garbled (and still looks like a key), and in an answer it goes into the model's context and transcript. A single-use link (below) puts them on disk without them passing through an answer;
  • tunnel_urls: the app addresses.

If status is not running, wake the sandbox and poll until it is:

POST /sandboxes/p9m-shop/start
GET  /sandboxes/p9m-shop        → repeat until "status": "running"

Waking from exited takes a few seconds; from deep_sleep about 30 seconds. Connecting to the Docker daemon does not wake it: while the sandbox sleeps, docker fails to connect (connection reset or EOF), so wake it first.

A request to an app address while the sandbox is not ready returns an HTML waiting page ("Sandbox is waking up") with status 200, instead of the real answer: treat it as "not ready yet" and retry after a few seconds.

docs.title: 2. Connect the docker command line
docs.text:
Ask for a single-use link to the project's .p9m folder (MCP: project_dir_link). Purgatorium checks the keys first; the link works once, for 5 minutes:

POST /sandboxes/p9m-shop/project-link
→ { "url": "https://p9m.example.com/project-dir/…", "expires_in": 300,
    "command": "curl -sf \"https://p9m.example.com/project-dir/…\" | tar -x -C <project folder>",
    "context_commands": ["docker context rm -f p9m-shop", "docker context create p9m-shop --docker \"host=tcp://shop-docker.example.com:443,ca=<project folder>/.p9m/docker/ca.pem,…\""] }

Run command, then context_commands, with the project's root folder for <project folder>. The download writes .p9m/.gitignore (*: git leaves the folder out), .p9m/p9m.env (P9M_URL, P9M_SANDBOX, P9M_DOCKER_HOST) and .p9m/docker/{ca,cert,key}.pem. On Windows: curl.exe --ssl-no-revoke; tar comes with Windows 10 and later. A used or expired link answers 410: ask for a new one.

docker --context p9m-shop compose ls

A context keeps its own copies of the files: after new keys run both again, with a new link. Check it with a compose command, as above: ps can work with a key that compose cannot read (tls: failed to parse private key). On a TLS error get a new link; do not repair a key file. Add .p9m to .dockerignore, so that a build never copies the keys into an image.

Only TLS with these certificates gets in: Purgatorium passes the connection through without opening it. Keep the key as secret as the token.

If the user gave you an export instead, it is a .p9m folder for the project's root folder (from the zip p9m-<sandbox>.zip; an older export is a p9m-<sandbox>/ folder): p9m.env, docker/ with the certificates, a README, and a .gitignore of * that keeps the folder out of git. p9m.env has P9M_DOCKER_HOST. Unpack a zip into the project's root and delete the zip (it holds a token); add .p9m to .dockerignore, so that a build never copies the keys into an image:

docker context create p9m-shop --docker "host=$P9M_DOCKER_HOST,ca=$PWD/.p9m/docker/ca.pem,cert=$PWD/.p9m/docker/cert.pem,key=$PWD/.p9m/docker/key.pem"

docs.title: 3. Deploy an app
docs.text:
A compose project in the sandbox, built and run there:

docker --context p9m-shop compose -p shop up -d --build

services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    labels:
      p9m.subdomain: shop
  • Publish ports on all interfaces (8080:8080): that is what gives the app its public address. A port published on 127.0.0.1 stays private to the sandbox: no address at all. The app itself must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside its container (not 127.0.0.1), or its address answers with an error; GET /sandboxes/:name → apps[].answers says whether it answers. An app labelled p9m.access: domain or owner (App access) answers your own curl with a redirect to Purgatorium's sign-in: check apps[].answers instead. Without a label an app opens only for its owner (the server's default, unless it sets another): set the label the user asks for (for my colleagues → domain, for anyone → public, e.g. a webhook receiver) before the first deploy.
  • Set a restart policy (restart: unless-stopped): when the sandbox wakes from sleep, only containers with one start again.
  • Pass secrets when the container runs (environment:, env_file: read on your machine by docker compose), never in the image.

docs.title: The app's public address
docs.text:
Every published TCP port gets an HTTP address. With the sandbox p9m-shop on example.com:

  • with a p9m.subdomain: shop label: https://shop-shop.example.com, that is <sandbox>-<subdomain>.<domain>;
  • without the label: https://shop-<project>-<container>-port<host port>.example.com. The container name is <project>-<service>-1 unless container_name is set.

The app is reachable a few seconds after the container starts. GET /sandboxes/p9m-shop lists the addresses in tunnel_urls.

A database or other TCP service published the same way also gets a TLS address on port 443: see Isolation and TCP addresses.

docs.title: 4. Update the app
docs.text: Change the code or the image tag and run the same docker --context p9m-shop compose -p shop up -d --build again: compose recreates the changed containers and keeps the volumes. Use a fixed tag for every release (:1.4.2, :1.4.3, …) so you can roll back by deploying the previous one.

docs.title: Push to the registry
docs.text:
Every sandbox can push to Purgatorium's registry, so an image can be pulled elsewhere too:

docker login registry.example.com -u shop             # password: the token
docker --context p9m-shop tag shop-web registry.example.com/shop/web:3
docker --context p9m-shop push registry.example.com/shop/web:3
  • Every push is scanned for secrets, and an image with a .env file or a key in it stays private (GET /sandboxes/<name>/registry shows what was found).
  • Anyone can pull the image from any machine (docker pull registry.<domain>/shop/web:3) once every version of it passed the scan: one flagged version keeps the whole image private until it is deleted.

docs.title: 5. Other ways in
docs.text:
• SSH: ssh root@<sandbox>-shell-tcp.<domain> through port 443 (SSH, terminal and logs); inside, docker talks to the sandbox's Docker.
  • Logs of every app in the sandbox: GET /sandboxes/<name>/logs/stream (Server-Sent Events).
  • Move the work itself into the sandbox: with the Claude Code plugin, /p9m:teleport puts the project, its confirmed secrets and the conversation into a claude container next to the apps, to continue there (Claude Code plugin).

docs.title: With Portainer
docs.text:
A sandbox made from the portainer template (or one with Portainer in its own compose) also has Portainer, which proxies the sandbox's Docker daemon over HTTPS: an agent can deploy through its API without the docker command line. GET /sandboxes/<name> then has:

  • extras.portainer_url, for example https://shop-portainer.example.com (if its host is not in tunnel_urls, Portainer is published on 127.0.0.1 and private to the sandbox: ask the user to publish it on all interfaces, 9000:9000, in Starter stack…);
  • extras.portainer_password (user admin).

GET <portainer_url>/api/status returning JSON means Portainer is ready (an HTML answer is the waiting page). Portainer traffic wakes an asleep sandbox and keeps it awake.

docs.title: Sign in to Portainer
docs.text:
If p9m.env has P9M_PORTAINER_URL and P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN, skip the sign-in: use P9M_PORTAINER_URL as <portainer_url> and send X-API-Key: <P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN> instead of Authorization: Bearer <jwt> on every Portainer call below. (A line # Portainer: not included (…) says why there is none; then sign in as below, or use the Docker command line, 2.)

Otherwise sign in with extras.portainer_password:

POST <portainer_url>/api/auth
Content-Type: application/json

{"username": "admin", "password": "<extras.portainer_password>"}

The answer is {"jwt": "…"}. Send Authorization: Bearer <jwt> on every Portainer call below.

Then find the environment (endpoint) ID. It is the sandbox's Docker daemon, usually 1:

GET <portainer_url>/api/endpoints      → [{"Id": 1, "Name": "primary", …}]

If the list is empty (nobody clicked Get started in the Portainer UI yet), create the environment once:

POST <portainer_url>/api/endpoints
Content-Type: multipart/form-data

Name=local
EndpointCreationType=1

docs.title: Deploy an app as a stack
docs.text:
A Portainer stack is a compose project that Portainer can update later. Deploy it from compose text:

POST <portainer_url>/api/stacks/create/standalone/string?endpointId=1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "shop",
  "stackFileContent": "services:\n  web:\n    image: registry.example.com/shop:1.4.2\n    ports: [\"8080:8080\"]\n    labels:\n      p9m.subdomain: shop\n",
  "env": [{"name": "LOG_LEVEL", "value": "info"}]
}

The answer includes the stack Id; keep it for updates. GET <portainer_url>/api/stacks lists the stacks with their IDs.

The same rules hold as in 3. Deploy an app: publish ports on all interfaces, set a restart policy.

docs.title: Update a stack
docs.text:
Change the image tag in the compose text and redeploy. pullImage: true pulls the image again even if the tag did not change (for :latest):

PUT <portainer_url>/api/stacks/<stack id>?endpointId=1
Content-Type: application/json

{"stackFileContent": "<the full compose text>", "env": [], "prune": true, "pullImage": true}

prune: true removes services that are no longer in the compose text. Portainer recreates the changed containers; the volumes are kept.

To build in the sandbox, send the build context as a tar archive to the Docker build endpoint through Portainer's Docker proxy:

POST <portainer_url>/api/endpoints/1/docker/build?t=shop:1.4.3
Content-Type: application/x-tar

<tar of the directory with the Dockerfile>

The answer streams the build log as JSON lines; the last line is {"stream":"Successfully tagged shop:1.4.3\n"} on success, or an {"error": …} line on failure. Then redeploy the stack with image: shop:1.4.3 and pullImage: false (the image only exists locally).

docs.title: Everything else Docker can do
docs.text:
<portainer_url>/api/endpoints/1/docker/<Docker Engine API path> is the sandbox's Docker Engine API. Examples:

Call Docker Engine API GET …/docker/containers/json list running containers GET …/docker/containers/<name>/logs?stdout=1&stderr=1&tail=200 container logs POST …/docker/containers/<name>/restart restart a container POST …/docker/images/create?fromImage=alpine&tag=3.20 pull an image DELETE …/docker/images/<image> remove an image

The stack Purgatorium deployed when it created the sandbox (Portainer + http-echo) was deployed with docker compose outside Portainer: Portainer shows it but cannot edit it as a stack.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Sleep: the sandbox sleeps after its idle timeout without HTTP traffic, 30 minutes by default. The user can change this or turn it off in the UI (Sleep settings…) or with PATCH /sandboxes/<name> {"idle_timeout": "2h"}, where 0 or off means never. Docker traffic keeps a running sandbox awake (a build, docker logs -f, a pull), but a connection that is only open does not; plain HTTP traffic to its apps (or to Portainer) counts too.
  • Archive (DELETE /sandboxes/<name>, Archive… in the UI) archives the sandbox: its configuration and data are kept in the archive, and it is removed from the list.
  • The Purgatorium API reference is at <Purgatorium URL>/swagger.

docs.title: Let your agent deploy
docs.text:
Give a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…) a personal access token and a sandbox, and it can ship your app there on its own: wake the sandbox, deploy a compose project to the sandbox's own Docker daemon, build images inside it, read the logs and roll out new versions. The app gets its public URL from the tunnel.

  1. In the UI: create a sandbox (say shop), then in its panel's Access tab Token for this sandbox… — a token that works only for that sandbox.
  2. Download p9m.env in the token's dialog and save it in your project folder (keep it out of git), then tell the agent: Deploy this app to my Purgatorium sandbox — settings in p9m.env. The file holds P9M_URL, P9M_TOKEN, P9M_SANDBOX and P9M_AGENT_GUIDE. Or tell the agent everything yourself, for example:

Deploy this repo to my Purgatorium sandbox p9m-shop at https://p9m.example.com with the token p9m_…. Follow https://csakaszamok.github.io/p9m/latest/agent-guide/index.md.

docs/agent-guide.md is written for the agent: every call it needs, tried against a live Purgatorium. A token limited to one sandbox keeps the agent away from your other sandboxes; a token for all your sandboxes (Access tokens → + New token) acts as you.

An agent with MCP can also use Purgatorium as an MCP server with the same token: see MCP. In Claude Code, the p9m plugin needs no token typed in: install it once (/plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m, /plugin install p9m@p9m), then run /p9m:init <address> in the project (a new sandbox; /p9m:init <address> <sandbox> for one you have), approve in the browser and paste back the code it shows.

docs.title: Docker, registry, export
docs.text:
A coding agent (Claude Code, Codex…) can work on a sandbox with plain docker commands:

  • Docker from outside: <raw>-docker.<domain>:443 reaches the sandbox's own Docker daemon. Purgatorium does not open that TLS: it only reads the name and passes the connection through, so the Docker command line and the sandbox talk to each other with the sandbox's own certificates (only whoever holds its client key gets in). It does not wake a sleeping sandbox (wake it first: Wake, POST /sandboxes/:name/start, or the MCP tool wake_sandbox); traffic on the connection keeps a running one awake, a connection that is only open (e.g. Docker Desktop keeping a context connected) does not.
  • Let your agent deploy…, on a sandbox's App ports tab (and in the Advanced view also at the top of its Access tab), is the same window in both views. For the Claude Code plugin: the two lines that install it (once), and the /p9m:init <address> <sandbox> line to paste into Claude Code in the project; you approve in the browser, and the project gets its .p9m folder with a token for the sandbox. For other agents: Download gives p9m-<raw>.zip, with a .p9m folder to unpack in the project's root folder (its own .gitignore of * keeps it out of git; add .p9m to .dockerignore too, so that a build never copies it into an image), and what to tell the agent (set up the p9m zip from my Downloads in this project and deploy). Before a sandbox has Docker access it offers to enable it, or to export without the Docker keys. In the Advanced view the window has Options: the token's name and expiry (for the zip), a zip without the Docker keys, and Copy as .env, which puts p9m.env (a new token for the sandbox) on the clipboard. When the sandbox's Portainer is public, both also carry P9M_PORTAINER_URL and a Portainer API token (P9M_PORTAINER_TOKEN, sent as X-API-Key), made for the export, so the agent never gets the Portainer admin password; making it wakes the sandbox. That token does not expire and revoking the Purgatorium token does not revoke it: delete it in the sandbox's Portainer (My account → Access tokens). The .p9m folder holds p9m.env (with a new token limited to the sandbox, P9M_DOCKER_HOST, P9M_REGISTRY), the Docker client keys and a README with the docker context create command for Windows and macOS/Linux. It is a secret; Rotate Docker keys… makes the keys of earlier exports useless.
  • Registry: docker login registry.<domain> with a Purgatorium token as the password (a token limited to a sandbox pushes to <raw>/…, a personal one to its owner's sandboxes); the password returned at create still works.
  • Anonymous pull after a secret scan: every push is scanned (files such as .env, private keys, and well-known key formats, in every layer and in the image config, where Dockerfile ENV lines end up). Anonymous pull is decided per repository: one whose versions are all clean — and that has nothing in the registry Purgatorium has not scanned — can be pulled by anyone without logging in; one flagged, unscanned or failed version keeps the whole repository private until it is deleted. The registry tells Purgatorium about pushes with a secret Purgatorium generates (data/registry-notify.secret). Garbage collection runs weekly; a push at that very moment may fail and needs a retry. The Registry tab shows the images, the scan results (masked) and a Delete button. REGISTRY_PUBLIC_PULL=false keeps everything private.

docs.title: An agent inside a sandbox
docs.text:
A coding agent can also run inside one sandbox (say, in a VS Code or code-server container there) and deploy to another: give it that other sandbox's access as usual (the Claude Code plugin with /p9m:init for that sandbox, or its zip). It needs two names to reach from inside the sandbox: Purgatorium's (p9m.<domain>, the API and MCP) and the other sandbox's Docker address (<sandbox>-docker.<domain>), plus its apps' addresses if it opens them.

With a real domain (a wildcard DNS record for *.<domain>), these names point at the server from inside a sandbox too: nothing to set. The server must reach its own public address from inside, which it usually does ("hairpin NAT"; most clouds and Docker do it).

On a local development stack on lvh.me they do not: lvh.me names point at 127.0.0.1, which inside a sandbox's container is that container itself, not Purgatorium. With Docker Desktop (Windows, macOS), point them at the host, 192.168.65.254 (what host.docker.internal resolves to; a fixed address), with extra_hosts on the agent's service in that sandbox's compose file:

    extra_hosts:
      - "p9m.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"
      - "shop-docker.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"   # the other sandbox's Docker address
      - "shop-web.lvh.me:192.168.65.254"      # its app, if the agent opens it

It has to be an address: extra_hosts takes no names, and host-gateway inside a sandbox is the sandbox's own container, not the host. The names stay as they are, because the TLS certificates and Traefik's routing go by them. On a Linux host without Docker Desktop there is no such address: use a real domain there.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method Path Description POST /sandboxes Create a sandbox (name, or none for a generated one like k3x9q2; optional runtime like dind, template like starter (its starter stack as it is: a compose text is refused), idle_timeout like 30m, deep_sleep_after like 7d or off, ssh_keys (extra SSH public keys for this sandbox only), cpus like 2, memory like 4g, create_inner_stack: false for no template stack) GET /sandboxes List all sandboxes GET /sandboxes/summary How many sandboxes: quota, total, free, running, asleep, deep_sleep, archived; your own (and server_full), or for the admin the whole server, by_owner, server_limit / server_used and resources (not with a token limited to one sandbox) GET /sandboxes/:name Get sandbox details; the Docker client certificates and key (ca_cert, client_cert, client_key) only with ?include_keys=true GET /sandboxes/:name/compose The starter stack deployed into the sandbox (compose YAML), secrets masked (Starter stack… in the UI) PATCH /sandboxes/:name Change idle_timeout and/or deep_sleep_after (see Sleep and wake), cpus and/or memory (see CPU and memory) GET /sandbox-name A free name for a new sandbox ({"name": "k3x9q2"}): what New sandbox fills in POST /sandboxes/:name/start Wake a sandbox, also from deep sleep (Wake in the UI); 409 at the owner's limit with reason and running; {"sleep": "<name>"} puts that running one to sleep first POST /sandboxes/:name/stop Put a sandbox to sleep now (Sleep in the UI) POST /sandboxes/:name/deep-sleep Put a sandbox into deep sleep now, also a running one (Deep sleep now on the panel's Details tab) POST /sandboxes/:name/keep-awake Start a running sandbox's sleep countdown over (Reset next to Sleeps in); 409 if it is not running POST /sandboxes/:name/export A zip for coding agents: a new token for the sandbox, its Docker client keys, a README (owner/admin; not with a token limited to one sandbox); docker: false without the keys, format: "env" the p9m.env text POST /sandboxes/:name/project-link A single-use link (5 minutes) to the project's .p9m folder with the Docker client keys, checked first; answers url, command (curl … \| tar -x) and context_commands, never the keys GET /project-dir/:token The .p9m folder as a tar, once (no token: the link is the authorization); 410 when used or expired POST /device/code Start a device approval for /p9m:init (no token): sandbox for one of the user's, or none for a new one, from template (or the default; not with sandbox; an unknown one is 400). Answers device_code (the agent's secret), user_code, verification_uri_complete and expires_in (600) POST /device/token Hand in the confirmation code the approval page showed (no token; device_code and code in the body): approved with the same answer as project-link and name, the sandbox as the user knows it (shop for p9m-shop), once; 400 {"status": "wrong", "tries_left"} (5 wrong ones end it), 403 denied, 409 pending, 410 expired (also used or ended). The approval resets the 10 minutes GET /activate The page where a signed-in user approves or denies a code (?code=): access to the named sandbox, or a new one; POST sends the decision, creates the new sandbox (as POST /sandboxes) and shows the confirmation code POST /sandboxes/:name/docker-keys New Docker access certificates (Enable / Rotate Docker keys…); restarts the sandbox GET /sandboxes/:name/registry The sandbox's images in the registry, with secret-scan results DELETE /sandboxes/:name/registry/:app/:digest Delete one version of an image POST /sandboxes/:name/restart Restart a sandbox GET /sandboxes/:name/files List a folder of the sandbox's files (path, default /root): /root, /home, /srv and /opt, the folders kept over a deep sleep, and the apps' volumes; the sandbox must be running (409 not_running otherwise). See Files GET /sandboxes/:name/files/content Download a file (path), or a folder as a tar PUT /sandboxes/:name/files/content Upload a file to path (the body is the file; missing folders on the path are made), up to FILES_MAX_UPLOAD GET /sandboxes/:name/files/text A text file's content as JSON (UTF-8, up to 1 MB): for agents POST /sandboxes/:name/files/mkdir Create a folder ({"path": "/srv/data"}) DELETE /sandboxes/:name/files Delete a file or a folder (path), not the four folders themselves (nor a volume's folder) GET /sandboxes/:name/volumes The volumes of the apps in the sandbox's own Docker: name, path (for the routes above), project, containers that use it GET /sandboxes/:name/mounts The host folders mounted into the sandbox: mounts (host, target, readonly), enabled (HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS is set); the admin also gets roots. Owner, admin, and a token limited to the sandbox. See Host folders POST /sandboxes/:name/mounts Mount a host folder (admin only, HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS set, else 403 / 409): {"host": "/srv/shared/team", "target": "/mnt/team", "readonly": true}, target defaulting to /mnt/<last part of host>. The sandbox container is recreated (a running one restarts). 400 for a path outside the roots or a target that is not allowed; 409 with Docker's words when Docker refuses it (e.g. the host folder does not exist), nothing changed DELETE /sandboxes/:name/mounts?target=/mnt/team Unmount it (admin only; also with HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS unset); the sandbox container is recreated DELETE /sandboxes/:name Archive the sandbox, then remove it (Archive… in the UI; see Delete = archive) GET /runtimes List the runtimes new sandboxes may use (name, description, default; only those in ALLOWED_RUNTIMES when it is set) GET /templates List the templates (name, description, default) GET /ssh-keys Your SSH public keys (id, name, type, fingerprint, created_at) POST /ssh-keys Add a public key (key, optional name); it lets you into all your sandboxes with SSH GET /sandboxes/:name/ssh-key The sandbox's generated SSH private key (download) POST /sandboxes/:name/ssh-key Generate it for an SSH sandbox that has none yet GET /sandboxes/:name/containers The containers in the sandbox's own Docker: name, project, service, image, state, status, running ones first; the sandbox must be running (409 not_running otherwise) GET /sandboxes/:name/terminal The browser terminal (page; the same path as a websocket: the shell; ?container=<name>: in that container of the sandbox's own Docker) GET /sandboxes/:name/logs The logs page (signed-in browsers) GET /sandboxes/:name/logs/stream The sandbox's app logs as Server-Sent Events: the last 100 lines of every container, then live (token too) DELETE /ssh-keys/:id Delete one of your keys (it stops working at once) GET /templates/:name A template's compose.yaml as written (compose), to show before a create GET /me Who you are signed in as, Purgatorium's own address (url), your running sandboxes and limit, and server_places: the sandbox places on the server, used and limit (null without a server limit) PUT /me/view The web UI's view for this account: {"view": "simple"} or "advanced" (GET /me returns it as view, and whether the account may switch as view_switch); a user gets 403 unless USER_VIEW_SWITCH=true PUT /me/theme The web UI's theme for this account: {"theme": "light"}, "dark", or "system" to follow the device again (GET /me returns it as theme, null when the device decides); any account may set it GET /tokens List your personal access tokens (hint: the token's start and end, e.g. p9m_aB3x…9fQz; null for tokens made before hints) POST /tokens Mint a personal access token (name, optional expires_in like 30d/90d/never) DELETE /tokens/:id Revoke a personal access token GET /users Accounts (admin): first and last seen, last sign-in, sign-ins, sandboxes now and created, last API use DELETE /users/:account Forget an account's stats row (admin); the account and its sandboxes stay

All endpoints require Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN | personal token> or a signed-in browser session. Users only see their own sandboxes.

docs.title: OpenAPI and clients
docs.text:
The whole API is described as OpenAPI 3.0 at /swagger.json (no token needed to read it), and you can try it in Swagger UI at /swagger. There is no official SDK yet; generate a client in your language from that document instead, for example typed TypeScript:

curl -s https://p9m.example.com/swagger.json -o p9m.json
npx openapi-typescript p9m.json -o p9m.d.ts   # use it with openapi-fetch

or any language openapi-generator supports (openapi-generator-cli generate -i p9m.json -g python -o p9m-client). The document's version is Purgatorium's own, so regenerate after an upgrade.

More reading: architecture diagrams, how agents deploy, comparison with other sandbox platforms, roadmap.

docs.title: App access
docs.text:
By default a web app in a sandbox opens only for its sandbox's owner (and the admin): an app is made public on purpose, not by forgetting a label. A builder chooses, app by app, who opens it, with a label on the app's container:

p9m.access Who opens the app's web address public Anyone. domain Anyone who can sign in to this Purgatorium (its sign-in allowlist, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS and OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS), and the admin. owner The sandbox's owner, and the admin. 
services:
  admin:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    labels:
      p9m.access: public    # or domain; owner when there is no label

An app without the label gets the server's default, APPS_ACCESS_DEFAULT (owner unless set; a company may set domain; public is how it was before 0.12.12). A value that is not one of the three (a typo such as privat) means owner, and the sandbox's Details tab says so. The App ports tab marks each app that is not public: Owner only, Your domain.

docs.title: What a visitor sees
docs.text:
The first time someone opens an app that is not public, their browser makes a short hop to Purgatorium: they sign in if they are not signed in yet, and come straight back to the app. That gives them a cookie for that one app's address, for 8 hours. Someone who may not open it sees a page that says so (This app is open only to its owner) and which account they are signed in with.

Purgatorium's own sign-in never reaches an app: the cookie an app's address gets says only that this person may view this app, and Purgatorium takes it off every request before the app sees it, so an app cannot use it to act as its visitor.

An asleep app is woken only for someone who may open it: an anonymous visitor of an owner-only app gets the sign-in hop, not a waking sandbox.

docs.title: The app knows who is viewing
docs.text: Behind domain and owner, every request to the app carries X-P9m-User: <their e-mail> (admin for the admin). An app can greet its visitor with it, or use it as its own sign-in. Purgatorium removes an X-P9m-User that a visitor sends themselves, also for public apps, so the header can be trusted, but only behind Purgatorium.

docs.title: Not covered
docs.text:
• The TCP addresses (databases, SSH, Docker) are not HTTP: this does not apply to them. They are protected by their own TLS certificates and passwords, as before; see Isolation and TCP addresses.
  • Other sandboxes do not get a way around it since 0.12.23: a sandbox is on its own network, so another sandbox reaches its apps only through their addresses, like anyone (Isolation and TCP addresses).
  • Webhooks and API clients without a browser cannot make the sign-in hop. Keep an app that receives webhooks, or that a script or a mobile app calls, public for now.
  • A coding agent's own curl to an app that is not public gets the sign-in redirect. The agent checks whether an app answers from inside (GET /sandboxes/:name → apps[].answers), which is not affected.

docs.title: Timing and failures
docs.text:
• A new or changed label applies within about 12 seconds of the deploy (Purgatorium reads the running sandboxes' labels every 10 s; Traefik asks Purgatorium every 2 s). Until then the sandbox goes by what Purgatorium last knew of it: in a sandbox whose apps were all public, a newly deployed owner app (with the label, or without one) is open for those seconds. For an app that must never be open, not even briefly, publish its port on 127.0.0.1 first and on all interfaces only after a few seconds, or deploy it into a sandbox that already has a domain or owner app.
  • A sandbox whose apps are all public does not depend on Purgatorium while it runs, as before. One with a domain or owner app does: while Purgatorium is down, those apps do not open (it fails closed); public sandboxes keep working.
  • The check is per sandbox (one router serves all its apps): in a sandbox with a domain or owner app, its public apps also need Purgatorium. Keep an app that must stay reachable while Purgatorium is down (a webhook receiver, a status page) in a sandbox whose apps are all public.
  • If Traefik restarts while Purgatorium is down, no sandbox app opens until Purgatorium is back (Traefik has not yet read the access middlewares).

docs.title: On the Hub
docs.text: An owner-only app is not published on the Hub, even with p9m.publish (the Details tab says so: set p9m.access: domain). A domain app shows to Hub viewers who can sign in to Purgatorium itself; viewers who can sign in only to the Hub (HUB_ALLOWED_*) see the public apps.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Variable Default APPS_ACCESS_DEFAULT owner The level of an app without p9m.access: owner, domain or public. APP_ACCESS_SECRET generated Signs the app cookies and the one-time sign-in tickets. Without it Purgatorium generates one into data/app-access.key and keeps it.

docs.title: Delete = archive
docs.text:
DELETE /sandboxes/:name never discards data. It:

  1. stops the sandbox;
  2. writes every Docker volume of the sandbox's compose project to opt/archive/<owner>/<name>-<timestamp>/volumes/<volume>.tar.gz (the DinD data volume holds all inner images, containers and volumes, except claude_secrets, the secrets a project brought with /p9m:teleport: they never go into an archive, and a restored sandbox is teleported into again to get them);
  3. copies opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/ (compose files, certs, credentials) to .../config/ and writes manifest.json (with the owner, and secrets_excluded: true);
  4. only then removes the containers, the volumes and opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/ (and the owner's directory once it is empty). If any archive step fails nothing is removed and the call returns 500.

Afterwards the name is free again and the sandbox URL returns 404. Archives are never pruned automatically; expect a few hundred MB per sandbox, more with large images.

Restoring by hand:

A=opt/archive/alice@example.com/p9m-alice-2026-09-26T21-47-01-401Z
mkdir -p opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com
cp -r $A/config opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com/p9m-alice
for f in $A/volumes/*.tar.gz; do
  v=$(basename $f .tar.gz)
  docker volume create --label com.docker.compose.project=p9m-alice $v
  docker run --rm -v $v:/data -v "$PWD/$A/volumes":/archive alpine tar xzf /archive/$v.tar.gz -C /data
done
docker compose -f opt/sandboxes/alice@example.com/p9m-alice/docker-compose.yml up -d

docs.title: Claude Code plugin
docs.text:
New to this?

Put your app online with Claude Code walks through it step by step.

The p9m plugin teaches Claude Code to deploy: you say put my app online, it deploys the project to your sandbox's own Docker, checks that the app answers and gives you its address. The plugin itself keeps no address and no token: each project says which Purgatorium and which sandbox it belongs to, in its own .p9m folder.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Once on your computer, from a terminal (Purgatorium shows these lines once you sign in). Claude Code in an editor (the VS Code extension) has no /plugin, so there this is the way:

claude plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m

Or in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m
/plugin install p9m@p9m

Claude Code asks where to install it: user (every folder of yours; usually what you want), project (this repository, for everyone who uses it, through its .claude/settings.json) or local (this folder, only you). It asks for nothing else: no address, no token. Updates come with Purgatorium's releases (/plugin marketplace update p9m).

Installed the plugin when it was called p7y (/p7y:init)? Claude Code knows that one by its old name, and /plugin marketplace update p9m finds nothing. Remove it and add the new one, in a terminal, in the folder where you installed it:

claude plugin uninstall p7y@p7y --scope local
claude plugin marketplace remove p7y
claude plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m

--scope is where you installed it (claude plugin list shows it: user, project or local); a local one only from its own folder. Then start Claude Code again.

docs.title: Connect a project: /p9m:init
docs.text:
Users get their sandboxes here, not in a web UI: only the admin has one. In Claude Code, in the project's root folder:

/p9m:init https://p9m.example.com                      # a new sandbox, from the default template
/p9m:init https://p9m.example.com --template empty     # a new sandbox, from that template
/p9m:init https://p9m.example.com k3x9q2               # one of your sandboxes

Claude Code prints a link. Open it in your browser (sign in first if Purgatorium asks). The page shows a code and what Claude Code asks for (a new sandbox from a template, or access to the named one); check that the code is the one Claude Code printed and click Create and approve or Approve (or Deny). There is nothing to pick on the page: a new sandbox gets a generated name, and a name that is not one of yours is refused. Only the sandbox's owner (or the admin) can approve. A new sandbox counts against the same limits as any other, and gets Docker access at once.

After the approval the page shows a second code. Paste it into Claude Code: only with it does Claude Code get the token, so a link someone else started gets them nothing unless you also send them that code. Both codes work once, for 10 minutes; 5 wrong pastes end the request.

Then Claude Code unpacks the project's .p9m folder straight to disk: a new token for that sandbox only (in .p9m/p9m.env, 90 days) and the sandbox's Docker keys. The token never shows on the screen or in the chat. The folder keeps itself out of git; the token is named Claude Code init <date> (the admin sees and revokes it under Access tokens).

Run /p9m:init with the sandbox's name again whenever the token has expired or was revoked. A project can be tied to one sandbox at a time; another project in another folder can be tied to another sandbox, or to another Purgatorium.

docs.title: The .p9m folder
docs.text: The .p9m folder in the project's root folder says which Purgatorium and which sandbox the project belongs to: p9m.env (the address, the sandbox's name and its token) and the sandbox's Docker keys. /p9m:init writes it, or you unpack it from an export zip. It holds secrets, and it keeps itself out of git: its own .gitignore is a single *. Add .p9m to .dockerignore too, so that a build never copies it into an image; the agent does when it writes one.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
In your project's folder, ask in your own words, e.g. deploy this app to my sandbox or give me a link to show this to someone, or run /p9m:deploy. You need Docker installed on your machine (the build runs in the sandbox, but the docker command line talks to it). In a project without a .p9m folder, the agent tells you to run /p9m:init first.

The plugin has three skills:

  • /p9m:init: ties the project to a sandbox, as above;
  • /p9m:deploy: the steps of the agent guide in short, for an agent that may be talking to someone who is not a developer. It works from .p9m/p9m.env with the REST API, and gets fresh Docker keys through a single-use link (unpacked to the disk, so a key never passes through the model: copied by a model a key gets garbled, and it would end up in the transcript);
  • /p9m:teleport: moves the project into its sandbox, to continue there (below).

The plugin does not bring the MCP server. Purgatorium still has one, for other MCP clients: see MCP.

docs.title: Continue in the sandbox: /p9m:teleport
docs.text:
/p9m:teleport (or /p9m:teleport --ecc) moves the project you are working on, with this conversation, into a claude container in the project's own sandbox, next to its apps; there claude --resume picks the conversation up where it stopped. It shows first what would move and asks:

  • the files: the working folder as it is, uncommitted changes too; what .gitignore leaves out stays home (node_modules, build output; without git a built-in list);
  • secrets: files that look like secrets (.env, *.pem, credentials*.json, …) go only if you say yes to each, by name. In the sandbox they are in a volume of their own, readable only by the claude container (folders 700, files 600), with a symlink in their place in the project; the container has no address; an archive never holds them. The server's administrator can still read them, as everything on the server;
  • this conversation, and your portable settings: global CLAUDE.md, your skills, the enabled plugins (installed again from their marketplaces), the permissions. Not your MCP servers, hooks or env: they point at things on your machine;
  • not the Claude Code sign-in: sign in once in the container (claude, then /login); it stays there.

The files go straight to the sandbox's Docker with the project's keys (.p9m/docker): Purgatorium only wakes the sandbox. Then open the sandbox's panel → the claude container's terminal, cd into the folder it names and claude --resume <id>. It is one way: the local folder keeps the moment of the teleport; bring work back with git. --ecc starts the container from the image with ECC (only when the sandbox has no claude container yet). Teleporting the same project again asks before it replaces the sandbox's copy.

docs.title: Where it works
docs.text: The plugin works fully in Claude Code: in the terminal, and in the Claude desktop app's Code tab; also in Claude Code inside a sandbox, deploying to another one (on a local lvh.me stack see An agent inside a sandbox). Claude chat and Cowork can install it too (Customize → Plugins, add the marketplace p9m-team/p9m), but they cannot run commands on your computer, so there it does not do much. Without the plugin, any agent can deploy with an export (Let your agent deploy… on a sandbox) or a token: see Let your agent deploy.

docs.title: Why Purgatorium, and how it compares
docs.text: As of October 2026. What is said about other products comes from the public sources listed at the bottom, and can change quickly.

docs.title: What Purgatorium is for
docs.text:
A place where a team's apps run: the ones people build with AI agents or vibe-code in an afternoon. Everyone gets their own space, every app gets a URL colleagues can open, and what nobody uses costs nothing. On your own server, not in someone else's cloud.

Think of it as a self-hosted Vercel or Railway for the whole team: you hand an agent a p9m.env, it deploys a docker-compose.yml, and a minute later https://shop-web.example.com works.

docs.title: How teams do this today, and what goes wrong
docs.text: Today What goes wrong It runs on someone's laptop No URL to show it, it stops when the lid closes, and it only works on that machine. A cloud PaaS (Vercel, Railway, Render, Fly.io, Netlify) Every experiment is another project on the bill; code and data leave the company network; a multi-container stack (app + database + worker) has to be rebuilt service by service; Vercel runs request-driven functions, not always-on processes. One shared VPS with Docker or Portainer Everyone is on one Docker daemon: they see each other's containers, ports collide, one runaway stack slows everyone down, one wrong docker rm hits someone else. Coolify or Dokploy Built for running a team's production apps: an admin sets up projects, everything keeps running all the time, teams on one server still share the daemon. A VM for everyone Expensive while idle, and someone has to create, patch and clean up every one of them.

docs.title: What Purgatorium does instead
docs.text:
• Self-service, like a cloud PaaS. Anyone signs in (Google or any OIDC) and creates a sandbox; a quota and CPU / memory limits keep one person from taking the whole server.
  • Its own Docker for everyone. Every sandbox has its own Docker daemon: what an agent produces (docker-compose.yml with app, database, cache) runs as it is, and nobody sees or breaks anyone else's containers.
  • A URL for every app, automatically. Whatever a sandbox publishes gets https://<name>-<app>.<domain>; databases and SSH get a TLS address on port 443. No DNS, no proxy rules per app.
  • Idle costs nothing. A sandbox without traffic falls asleep and wakes on the next request; after a longer sleep its containers are freed. Twenty experiments, three in use: the server carries three.
  • Made for coding agents. Let your agent deploy… (the Claude Code plugin with /p9m:init, or a zip for any agent) gives the agent a token for that one sandbox, Docker access from outside and a registry login; every pushed image is scanned for secrets before anyone can pull it anonymously.
  • Your server, your data, no bill per app. One docker compose up on one Linux host, also inside a company network; no paid edition.
  • Nothing is lost. Delete archives the sandbox's configuration and data.

docs.title: Against a cloud PaaS (Vercel, Railway, Render, Fly.io)
docs.text:
Purgatorium gives a team what these give one developer, on hardware the team already has.

Vercel / Railway / Render / Fly.io Purgatorium Where it runs, where the data is Their cloud Your server, also inside a company network What you pay for Every project, service and its usage The server What you deploy Mostly one service per app (Vercel: request-driven functions, also from a Dockerfile); Fly.io's Docker Compose support is basic A whole docker-compose.yml, as it is, with its own Docker daemon Idle apps Railway, Render (free tier) and Fly.io can scale to zero; otherwise they run and are billed Sleep by default, wake on the next request Many people on one account A team plan; everyone sees the team's projects Everyone sees only their own sandboxes; tokens limited to one sandbox Production features Global edge, autoscaling, managed databases, backups, zero operations None of these: one host, you run it

Pick a cloud PaaS for an app in production that has to scale and be up at 3 a.m. without you. Pick Purgatorium for the many apps before that point: experiments, demos, internal tools, vibe-coded apps, test environments, and for whatever must not leave the company network.

docs.title: Against self-hosted tools (Coolify, Dokploy, Portainer)
docs.text:
These also run on your own server, but they are built for one team running its apps, not for many people each having their own space.

Purgatorium Coolify Dokploy Portainer CE Separation between teams on one server each sandbox has its own Docker daemon and network teams get their own servers; on a shared server the daemon is shared a shared daemon; members get access per project a shared daemon; roles (read-only, operator) only in the paid Business Edition What the dashboard hides, Docker also hides yes no no no Who creates an environment anyone, within a quota an admin or team member, in the team's project an admin, or a member given the permission an admin Idle apps sleep keep running keep running keep running Roles and access control free free (admin, member) free (owner, admin, member); custom roles in Enterprise basic in CE, RBAC paid For agents an MCP server, a Claude Code plugin, tokens limited to one sandbox an MCP server (/mcp; read-only at first, deploys in later releases) an MCP server (Dokploy/mcp, also deploys) none built in A preview per pull request not yet (roadmap) yes (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea) yes (GitHub) no

On a shared Docker daemon, anyone who may deploy an arbitrary compose file can, for example, bind-mount host paths or attach to another project's network: the separation in the dashboard does not reach the daemon.

They work well together: try and build in a Purgatorium sandbox, push the image to its registry, run it in production with Coolify or Dokploy. A Purgatorium sandbox can also have its own Portainer (the portainer template), for that sandbox's daemon alone.

docs.title: Looks similar, does a different job
docs.text:
These come up in the same searches ("sandbox", "dev environment", "AI agent"), but they solve another problem:

  • Coder, GitHub Codespaces, Gitpod / Ona, DevPod: a workspace for writing code (an IDE, a repo, a terminal), not a place where the finished app keeps running for others. They fit next to Purgatorium: write in Coder or on the laptop, run in Purgatorium. Coder also runs coding agents: Coder Tasks starts one (Claude Code among them) in a workspace of its own, which pauses when idle, and Coder Agents runs its own agent from the control plane, so the model's keys never enter the workspace; process-level network and command rules for agents (Agent Boundaries) are not in the free edition. What the agent builds lives as long as its workspace, without an address for colleagues.
  • E2B, Daytona, Docker Sandboxes, Modal, Northflank sandboxes, kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox, Alibaba OpenSandbox: they let an agent execute code in an isolated box for minutes or hours, driven from an SDK, usually inside a microVM. None of them is meant to keep a team's app online at a URL for weeks. Daytona is no longer open source: its development moved to a private codebase, and its AGPL repository is archived at v0.190.0 (a community fork, Nightona, carries it on).

docs.title: Where Purgatorium is weaker
docs.text:
1. Isolation is not yet a boundary against hostile code. The dind runtime runs the sandbox privileged: root inside a sandbox can escape to the host. That is fine for colleagues and their own agents, not for strangers. The sysbox runtime removes privileged and is used in production, but still shares the host's kernel; a Kata Containers runtime, a lightweight VM with its own kernel per sandbox, is on the roadmap.
  2. One host for now. No multi-host scheduling and no warm pool; a new sandbox takes about 10 seconds once its images are pulled (the first one on a new server a minute or two), a wake from deep sleep about 30. Kubernetes support is on the roadmap.
  3. Sleep stops the containers. On wake the stack restarts by its restart policies; what was only in memory is gone.
  4. Missing pieces: no teams yet (a sandbox has one owner), no hard disk quota (only a warning above a disk limit; CPU and memory limits exist), no egress rules, no SDK (a REST API with an OpenAPI document to generate a client from, the Docker CLI and agent-guide.md).
  5. A young, small project: no community yet, no external security audit.

docs.title: When to choose something else
docs.text:
• Production that must scale and stay up without you → a cloud PaaS, or Coolify / Dokploy on your own servers.
  • Untrusted code from strangers (public sign-up) → a microVM sandbox (E2B, Docker Sandboxes, Northflank), until Purgatorium has a Kata runtime.
  • Writing code in a cloud IDE → Coder or Codespaces.
  • An agent running short scripts from an SDK → E2B, Daytona (as a service) or agent-sandbox.
  • Coding agents for a large engineering team, with policies per process → Coder (its agent features beyond Tasks are partly paid).
  • GPU or ML work → Modal.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Main settings in .env:

Variable Default Description ADMIN_TOKEN — (required; setup.sh generates one) Bearer token with admin rights on the API. docker compose refuses to start without it ADMIN_USER, ADMIN_PASSWORD admin, — The local admin account of the UI; it can sign in only with ADMIN_LOGIN=on SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT 30m Signed out of the web UI after this long without doing anything: a click, a key (also in a browser terminal), a scroll, or opening a page starts the time again; the list's own refreshes do not. Two minutes before, a bar offers Stay signed in; afterwards the sign-in page, and after signing in back to the same page. A session ends after 7 days in any case. off: only the 7 days. Tokens are not affected ADMIN_LOGIN off on: the sign-in page has the Administrator sign-in form (also the Hub's). Off, the form is not shown and the password is not even checked: it is an emergency door, not the everyday way in (that is OIDC with OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS). Turn it on in .env, docker compose up -d (a restart does not read .env), sign in, then turn it off again. While on, Purgatorium warns at startup SESSION_SECRET — Signs the session cookie; a long random string HOST_DOMAIN lvh.me Every address is under it: the UI, the registry, the sandbox apps (needs a wildcard DNS record) APPS_DOMAIN <HOST_DOMAIN> The sandboxes' app, TCP, SSH and Docker addresses under a domain of their own, e.g. example.app beside HOST_DOMAIN=example.dev: the UI, the registry and the Hub stay under HOST_DOMAIN. Needs its own wildcard DNS record and certificate. See A separate domain for the apps HOST_ADDRESS localhost The host's address, put into the sandbox TLS certificates and used for the registry token URL when PUBLIC_URL is not set UI_HOST p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN> The UI's own address, e.g. console.example.com with HOST_DOMAIN=example.com: the sandbox apps stay <sandbox>-<subdomain>.example.com. Under HOST_DOMAIN, the wildcard DNS record and certificate cover it. Set PUBLIC_URL to it too, and register its /auth/callback with the OIDC provider. A sandbox whose apps' addresses would include it (a sandbox console with console-admin.example.com) cannot be created PUBLIC_URL http://<UI_HOST> The address of the UI as users see it; https://… turns on the HTTPS checks (see HTTPS) USER_HOST sbx.<HOST_DOMAIN> The users' own address, e.g. sbx.example.com beside UI_HOST=console.example.com: signing in, approving /p9m:init (/activate), the API and /mcp for their Claude Code, and signing in to the sandbox apps. UI_HOST is then the admin's: a user who signs in there is sent on to USER_HOST (signed in again by the provider, usually without a click), and the admin's pages on USER_HOST go to UI_HOST. The API answers on both, so a project's .p9m from before keeps working; new ones, the /activate links and the users' page name USER_HOST. Under HOST_DOMAIN the wildcard DNS record and certificate cover it; register its /auth/callback with the OIDC provider too. Sandboxes created before reach it by its public address; new ones through Traefik, as the UI. off, or the same as UI_HOST: off, everyone uses UI_HOST OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME — Sign-in for everyone but the admin (see Web UI and sign-in) OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS — (anyone) Who may sign in with OIDC, as comma lists: domains (example.com,partner.org, the exact domain, not its subdomains) and single addresses (guest@gmail.com). With OIDC on, one of them is required: with both empty Purgatorium refuses to start, unless OIDC_ALLOW_ANYONE=true. Checked at sign-in and on every request: someone taken off the list (after a restart) is signed out and their tokens stop working at once. The admin is never limited OIDC_ALLOW_ANYONE false true: OIDC without OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS / OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS lets anyone with an account at the provider sign in and create sandboxes (with Google, any Google account); Purgatorium starts so, with a warning in its log. Otherwise it refuses to start OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS — (none) Addresses (comma list) that are the admin when they sign in with OIDC in the browser, as the local admin is: all sandboxes, the Overview, users, no limits, host folders. They may sign in even if OIDC_ALLOWED_* leaves them out. Their tokens stay a user's. Taken off the list (after a restart), their session is a user's again at once. The local admin (ADMIN_USER) stays APPS_ACCESS_DEFAULT owner Who opens a sandbox app without a p9m.access label: owner (its sandbox's owner and the admin), domain (anyone who can sign in to Purgatorium) or public (anyone; the default before 0.12.12) (see App access) APP_ACCESS_SECRET generated into data/app-access.key Signs the app access cookies and sign-in tickets HUB_ENABLED false The Hub, the team's published apps at their own address: off unless true. HUB_HOST hub.<HOST_DOMAIN> The Hub's address. HUB_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, HUB_ALLOWED_EMAILS (empty) Who may look at the Hub besides the builders (OIDC_ALLOWED_*): viewers, who cannot sign in to Purgatorium itself. Empty: only builders. HUB_TITLE Hub Shown in the Hub's header. SANDBOX_QUOTA 3 Sandboxes a user may have running at once; asleep and deep-sleeping ones are not counted; 0 = unlimited SANDBOX_QUOTA_MAX (empty) How many a user may have running while the server has room, above the guaranteed SANDBOX_QUOTA (e.g. 10). Above the guarantee a new sandbox, or one woken, needs room to spare: every other owner must still be able to reach their guarantee (their running sandboxes hold their places already), and so must one newcomer. Waking from plain sleep takes no new place, so only this maximum counts. Nobody is ever put to sleep to make room. Empty: nothing above SANDBOX_QUOTA; 0: no maximum FILES_MAX_UPLOAD 100m The largest file the Files tab (and PUT /sandboxes/:name/files/content) takes, like 512m or 1g. Every request body is read into memory first, so this (plus 1 MB) is also the cap on any request: a larger one gets 413 SANDBOX_MAX_TOTAL 200 (setup.sh: the suggested number for the host) Running sandboxes on the whole server, the admin's included. The suggested number: twice as many as can all use their full SANDBOX_CPUS and SANDBOX_MEMORY at once (2 GB of memory kept for the rest), since most idle or sleep at any moment and a full server asks people to put theirs to sleep; at most as many as the disk holds at SANDBOX_DISK each. setup.sh writes it into a new .env in place of the example's 200, check-host.sh prints it, and the admin's Overview shows it under Host resources, with a warning when the limit set is well above it; asleep, deep-sleeping and archived ones take no place, so letting a sandbox sleep frees it for everyone. When it is reached nobody but the admin can create one or wake one: the admin is never refused, but its running sandboxes take places too; 0 = no limit. Each sandbox, asleep too, keeps a Docker network until it goes into deep sleep: the host's Docker address pools must have room for them (see check-host.sh) DEFAULT_RUNTIME auto Runtime for new sandboxes when a request names none: auto picks sysbox where the host has sysbox installed (no privileged container) and dind otherwise; or name one (see Runtimes and templates) ALLOWED_RUNTIMES sysbox Runtimes new sandboxes may use, as a comma list, or all. The privileged dind is for development only (Docker Desktop, a laptop): sysbox,dind there; the development compose file (docker-compose.dev.yml) allows all. Others are left out of GET /runtimes and the New sandbox form, and a create asking for one is a 400 (so is one without a runtime when the default is not allowed). Existing sandboxes keep running, sleeping and waking SANDBOX_CPUS, SANDBOX_MEMORY 2, 4g CPU and memory limit of every new sandbox (see CPU and memory) SANDBOX_MAX_CPUS, SANDBOX_MAX_MEMORY 4, 8g How far a user can raise their sandbox's limits; the admin can go up to the host SANDBOX_MAX_IDLE_TIMEOUT, SANDBOX_MAX_DEEP_SLEEP_AFTER — (no limit) How long a user's sandbox may stay awake without traffic, and asleep before deep sleep, at most (e.g. 2h, 1d); with a limit, never (off) is not allowed either. A template's longer default is cut to it; a sandbox that already has a longer value keeps it until it is changed. The admin is not limited SANDBOX_DISK 20g Disk use above which a sandbox is flagged; a warning only, see Disk HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS (empty: off) Host folders the admin may mount into a sandbox, as a comma list of absolute paths (e.g. /srv/shared,/data/projects): a mount's host path must be one of them or under one (/srv/shared2 is not under /srv/shared). Entries that are not absolute or have .. are ignored, with a warning at startup; / (the whole host) is allowed, with a warning. A mount gives whoever owns the sandbox that host folder, as root (read-only if mounted so), and to every app in it. Empty: nobody can add a mount; ones already there stay until the admin removes them. See Host folders LOGIN_CAPACITY on The sign-in page shows the sandbox places on the server: taken and free of SANDBOX_MAX_TOTAL, with a bar (orange from 90%, red when full). The page is public, so off hides it; nothing is shown without a server limit. Counted at most every 30 seconds GITHUB_STATS on The topbar links to the GitHub repo and shows Purgatorium's version, stars and forks; the admin also sees when a newer release is out (one of the running series, else a later series). The server fetches the counts and the releases at most once an hour (users' browsers never contact GitHub, and nothing about the installation is sent); off never asks GitHub, and the link and the version stay USER_VIEW_SWITCH false No effect since 0.13.0: users have no web UI. The admin can always switch (see Simple and Advanced) GITHUB_LINK on off takes the GitHub card out of the topbar (and GitHub is never asked for the counts) UI_TITLE Purgatorium Agentium The name at the top left, on the sign-in page and in the browser tab titles; none shows no name UI_LOGO Purgatorium's logo The logo next to the name and the browser tab icon, on the Hub too: an https:// address, or an image file in the container (.svg, .png, .jpg, .webp, .gif, .ico), e.g. /app/data/logo.png for ./data/logo.png, served as /assets/custom-logo; none shows no logo. Its height is fixed, its width follows the image DEFAULT_TEMPLATE starter Template for new sandboxes when a request names none. An old value such as dind-standard makes every create without a template fail with Unknown template DEEP_SLEEP_CHECK_INTERVAL 1m How often Purgatorium looks for sandboxes to take into deep sleep HOST_SANDBOXES_DIR auto-detected Host path of opt/sandboxes (every sandbox's compose file mounts from it). Set it only if auto-detection fails P9M_API_BIND 127.0.0.1 Interface of the direct plain-HTTP API port 8081: by default on the host only. 0.0.0.0 opens it to every network without TLS (tokens cross it readable): only on a trusted network. With PUBLIC_URL empty, docker clients on other machines get registry tokens from http://<HOST_ADDRESS>:8081, which needs it P9M_VERSION the release the docker-compose.yml came from The image version to run. Pin it only to stay on a version: an upgrade with a new docker-compose.yml then needs it changed too REGISTRY_PUBLIC_PULL true Images whose versions all passed the secret scan can be pulled without a login; false: tokens only REGISTRY_CACHE_TTL 720h (30 days) How long the sandboxes' Docker Hub cache (registry-cache) keeps an image, counted from its first download: pulling it again does not extend it, so an image is downloaded again once its time is up, even in the middle of a workshop. In hours (168h = 7 days); 0 keeps everything for ever (the cache only grows: watch the disk). Not in hours (e.g. 7d): the cache does not start, and the sandboxes pull from Docker Hub directly

docs.title: Deep sleep
docs.text:
A sandbox that has been asleep for deep_sleep_after (template field, default 7d, off disables; overridable per sandbox on create) is taken down with compose down: its containers and its network are removed, its volumes and opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/ stay. The volumes hold everything a user keeps: the sandbox's inner Docker (docker_data: images, inner containers and their volumes) and the sandbox's own /opt, /root, /home and /srv, so nothing written there is lost when the container is recreated (deep sleep, or a container removed by hand). Anything else in the sandbox container's file system (e.g. packages installed with apk add) is not kept. This frees Docker networks, which are limited. Purgatorium checks every DEEP_SLEEP_CHECK_INTERVAL (default 1m).

The panel's Details tab says when a sandbox that is asleep or in deep sleep last ran (Last ran: 3 weeks ago; last_running_at in GET /sandboxes/:name), and so do its apps on the Hub. Purgatorium keeps that time when it takes the sandbox down; for one taken down before it did, the time is an estimate, marked ~.

Requests for a deep-sleeping sandbox have no sandbox router, so they reach Purgatorium's catch-all /wake, which rebuilds the stack (compose up) and shows a waiting page that updates until the app answers — usually 20–60 s. From then on Sablier handles it as usual. The API reports such sandboxes with status: "deep_sleep", and POST /sandboxes/:name/start (Wake in the UI) brings them up. Deep sleep now on the panel's Details tab (POST /sandboxes/:name/deep-sleep) takes a sandbox down right away, without waiting for deep_sleep_after.

An asleep sandbox whose containers point at a network that no longer exists is taken down the same way at the next check, whatever its deep_sleep_after. This happens after docker compose down on the Purgatorium stack, which removes and re-creates traefik-net: without it, Sablier could never start the sandbox again (exit code 128, "network … not found") and its waiting page would spin forever. The next request rebuilds it on the current networks; its data volume is kept.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
The Files tab of a sandbox's panel shows its files: open folders, upload files (Upload…, or drop them on the list, several at once) or whole folders with everything in them (Upload folder…, or drop the folder; folders on the way that are not there yet are made, empty ones too when dropped), download a file, or a whole folder as a .tar (Download folder), make folders and delete.

It shows four folders, the ones that are kept when the sandbox goes into deep sleep or its container is recreated: /root (where it opens), /home, /srv and /opt. Anything else in the sandbox container is gone then, so it is not offered here.

docs.title: The apps' volumes
docs.text:
Volumes, next to the four folders, lists the volumes of the apps in the sandbox's own Docker (a database's data, an app's uploads), with their compose project and the containers that use them; open one to browse, upload and download as above. Their files are in the sandbox container already (the sandbox's Docker keeps them under /var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume>/_data, in the docker_data volume), so nothing extra is started, and they are kept over a deep sleep too. Only the local driver's volumes are shown; a container's own files outside its volumes are not (use docker cp in the sandbox for those).

  • A running app: while a container that uses the volume runs, the tab says so. A copy of a database's files taken while it runs may not be consistent, and the app may not expect files changed under it: stop it first (docker compose stop db in the sandbox), or use the database's own dump.
  • Owners: uploaded files and new folders belong to root, readable by everyone (0644). An app running as another user that has to write them needs a chown in the sandbox.
  • A volume's own folder cannot be deleted here: remove the volume with docker volume rm.

The sandbox has to be running: asleep, the tab offers to wake it. A file can be up to FILES_MAX_UPLOAD (100 MB by default, see Configuration).

docs.title: API and MCP
docs.text:
Method Path GET /sandboxes/:name/files?path=/root/app The folder's entries (folders first): name, type (dir, file, link, other), size, mtime GET /sandboxes/:name/files/content?path=… A file's bytes, or a folder as a tar PUT /sandboxes/:name/files/content?path=… Upload: the body is the file (curl -T report.pdf); missing folders on the path are made GET /sandboxes/:name/files/text?path=… A text file as { path, text } (UTF-8, up to 1 MB) POST /sandboxes/:name/files/mkdir {"path": "/srv/data"} DELETE /sandboxes/:name/files?path=… A file, or a folder with everything in it GET /sandboxes/:name/volumes The apps' volumes: name, path (e.g. /var/lib/docker/volumes/shop_db/_data, for the routes above), project, containers (name, service, running, mount) 
curl -T notes.md -H "Authorization: Bearer $P9M_TOKEN" "https://p9m.example.com/sandboxes/p9m-shop/files/content?path=/root/notes.md"

A token limited to the sandbox may use all of them. Over MCP they are list_sandbox_files, read_sandbox_file, write_sandbox_file (text), create_sandbox_folder, delete_sandbox_file and list_sandbox_volumes; a download is left out, since a tool result carries no file.

docs.title: First sandbox
docs.text:
# Create a sandbox
curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/sandboxes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "alice", "idle_timeout": "30m"}'

# Response (abridged)
{
  "name": "p9m-alice",
  "tunnel_urls": ["alice-inner-http-echo-port5678.lvh.me", "..."],
  "registry_url": "registry.lvh.me",
  "registry_username": "alice",
  "registry_password": "...",
  "docker_access": { "host": "alice-docker.lvh.me", "state": "ready" },
  "extras": {}
}

Sign in at http://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN> to create sandboxes in the browser or mint a personal access token for your agents.

With "template": "portainer" the sandbox also gets Portainer, and extras has its portainer_url and portainer_password.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text:
Purgatorium serves HTTPS with a certificate you copy in (no automatic issuing):

  1. Copy a wildcard certificate for *.<HOST_DOMAIN> (ideally also <HOST_DOMAIN>; with an APPS_DOMAIN, *.<APPS_DOMAIN> too, in the same certificate) to certs/tls.crt (PEM, full chain: certificate + intermediates) and its key to certs/tls.key (PEM, unencrypted). certs/ is git-ignored.
  2. Set PUBLIC_URL=https://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN> and strong ADMIN_TOKEN, SESSION_SECRET and ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env.
  3. docker compose up -d p9m traefik. At startup Purgatorium writes dynamic/tls.yml (the certificate + an HTTP→HTTPS redirect for every host); Traefik serves the UI, API, registry and every sandbox app on port 443.

To renew, overwrite the two files and run docker compose restart traefik. Remove them and restart Purgatorium (docker compose up -d p9m) to go back to plain HTTP.

docs.title: Trying it locally with HTTPS (e.g. on Windows)
docs.text:
With PUBLIC_URL=https://p9m.lvh.me but no certificate in certs/, Traefik answers with its own self-signed one: the browser says Not secure, and although you can click through for the pages, it refuses the connections pages open themselves — the browser Terminal stays disconnected. (lvh.me and every *.lvh.me resolve to 127.0.0.1, so nothing else is needed.) Make a certificate your machine trusts with mkcert. In PowerShell:

winget install FiloSottile.mkcert
# winget changes PATH for new shells only: pick it up in this one
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine') + ';' + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User')
mkcert -install                     # adds a local CA to Windows' trusted roots (confirm the dialog)
cd <your p9m checkout>
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force certs | Out-Null
mkcert -cert-file certs\tls.crt -key-file certs\tls.key "*.lvh.me" lvh.me
docker compose restart p9m traefik

Then close the browser completely and open https://p9m.lvh.me again. On macOS / Linux the same with brew install mkcert / your package manager, and certs/tls.crt, certs/tls.key. The TLS TCP addresses (psql, SSH) use this certificate too, so their self-signed certificate warnings go away. Firefox keeps its own trust store: mkcert -install covers it when certutil (NSS tools) is installed.

The direct plain-HTTP API port 8081 is reachable only on the host (P9M_API_BIND=127.0.0.1, the default since 0.14.0): keep it so in a public deployment — with PUBLIC_URL set, docker clients get registry tokens from $PUBLIC_URL/v2/auth, i.e. over HTTPS.

With an https:// PUBLIC_URL, Purgatorium refuses to start while ADMIN_TOKEN or SESSION_SECRET is a default or .env.example value (or SESSION_SECRET is unset), or ADMIN_PASSWORD is while ADMIN_LOGIN=on. A running sandbox whose address no router matches shows "This address does not reach the sandbox" instead of an endless waiting page.

docs.title: Hub
docs.text:
The Hub lists the apps your team has built, in one place, for the people who use them: colleagues who never run a sandbox find an app and open it with one click. It is a web app of its own, at its own address (by default hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>), served by Purgatorium but apart from its UI: no sandboxes, no New sandbox, no quota.

An app appears on the Hub when a label on its container says so; it shows its title, description, owner and whether it runs or sleeps, and Open opens it in a new tab. An app that is asleep wakes on that click, as any request wakes it.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
# .env
HUB_ENABLED=true
# HUB_HOST=hub.example.com     # default: hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>
# HUB_TITLE=Example Ltd        # shown in its header

then docker compose up -d. HTTPS uses the same wildcard certificate as everything else under the domain.

Single sign-on: add https://hub.<HOST_DOMAIN>/auth/callback at your provider as a second allowed redirect URI (next to Purgatorium's https://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN>/auth/callback). The administrator can also sign in to the Hub with the password, so it can be tried without single sign-on.

docs.title: Who sees it
docs.text:
Who Settings May Builders OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS use Purgatorium, create sandboxes, publish, and use the Hub Viewers HUB_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, HUB_ALLOWED_EMAILS sign in to the Hub only
  • With HUB_ALLOWED_* empty, only builders (and the administrator) use the Hub.
  • A viewer who tries Purgatorium's own sign-in is refused with "You have access to the Hub only: https://hub.example.com", and gets no Purgatorium session or token.
  • Taken off a list: signed out of the Hub at the next request.

docs.title: Publish an app
docs.text:
Add labels to its container in the stack you deploy into the sandbox:

services:
  web:
    image: my-stock-room
    ports: ["8080:8080"]          # on all interfaces: it needs a web address
    labels:
      p9m.publish: "true"         # "true" or "1" publishes; anything else does not
      p9m.title: "Stock room"     # optional, at most 80 characters; default: the service name
      p9m.description: "Who took what from the stock room"   # optional, at most 280

  • A description over several lines keeps its line breaks on the Hub (YAML's |):

    p9m.description: |
  Who took what from the stock room.
  Ask Anna for access.

  • An image on its card: p9m.image: "/screenshot.png", a path inside the app (PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, at most 2 MB and 4096 × 4096 pixels). Without it the Hub uses the page's own <meta property="og:image"> if it has one, and otherwise the title's first letter on a colour. Purgatorium fetches the image in the background straight from the sandbox, only while the app runs (it never wakes an app for it), refreshes it once a day or when the label changes, and never fetches anything from another site: a URL in the label, or an og:image on another host, is ignored.

  • What is published is the app's web address, the one its sandbox's Apps tab shows; with several ports, the lowest one published on all interfaces. A published container with no such port is not on the Hub: the sandbox's Details tab warns published, but has no web address.
