  • It appears on the Hub within half a minute, without approval. Remove the label (and deploy again) to take it off; archiving the sandbox does too. Deep sleep keeps it on the Hub.
  • Apps started by hand or by an agent count as well: Purgatorium reads the labels from the sandbox's own Docker.
  • On the Apps tab, a published app has an On the Hub marker.

docs.title: Votes
docs.text: Everyone signed in to the Hub can vote for an app once (👍), their own too (as a GitHub star), and take the vote back. The Hub sorts by votes (Popular) or by date (New); only the count is shown, not who voted. Votes stay when an app leaves the Hub and count on if it is published again at the same address.

docs.title: Feed
docs.text:
The Hub has an RSS feed (/feed.xml) and a JSON Feed (/feed.json), so a new app shows up by itself where the team looks: a Slack, Teams or Mattermost channel (their RSS integrations), Linkwarden, an RSS reader, or n8n and bots for anything else.

Readers cannot sign in, so the feed takes a secret key: the administrator creates the link in Purgatorium's Overview → Hub feed → Create feed link. Only the key's hash is kept, so the link is shown once; creating a new one ends the old link. Without the key the feed answers 404.

docs.title: Not yet
docs.text: A webhook on new apps, a Hub per team (with teams), and a Hub open on the internal network without signing in are on the roadmap.

docs.title: App access
docs.text: An app open only to its owner (p9m.access: owner, see App access) is not published, even with p9m.publish: its Details tab says so. A domain app shows to Hub viewers who can sign in to Purgatorium itself; viewers allowed only on the Hub (HUB_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, HUB_ALLOWED_EMAILS) see public apps only. Opening a domain app makes the usual sign-in hop.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
No git clone is needed: every file comes from a GitHub release, and the image carries the rest.

First check the machine; it changes nothing (give it the HOST_DOMAIN you plan to use):

curl -fsSL https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/check-host.sh | bash -s -- dev.example.com

Or download it, read it, then run it:

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/check-host.sh
less check-host.sh
bash check-host.sh dev.example.com

Then, on a Linux host with Docker Engine, the compose plugin (Compose 2.17 or newer) and sysbox (without it no sandbox can be created: the privileged dind runtime is for development only):

mkdir p9m && cd p9m
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/docker-compose.yml
curl -fsSL https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/setup.sh | bash -s -- dev.example.com   # .env with your domain and random secrets
docker compose up -d

The directory must be called p9m: the compose project name comes from it. For a given version, use releases/download/v0.5.0/… instead of releases/latest/download/….

check-host.sh checks Docker and Docker Compose, sysbox, the address pools, ports, disk and registry access, and changes nothing (its sysbox check runs one throw-away alpine container); with the HOST_DOMAIN you plan to use it also checks the DNS records and, if certs/ has one, the certificate. Lines marked ✘ must be fixed first, ⚠ are worth reading. Run it again in the p9m folder once Purgatorium is set up: it then also checks the security of its .env and of the host (the API port, the admin's password sign-in, default secrets, an open OIDC sign-in, HTTPS, other open ports, the firewall, automatic updates, SSH passwords), marks each problem with !, and lists them all again at the end under NOT SECURE.

setup.sh works in the current directory: it creates .env from its release's env.example, sets HOST_DOMAIN to the domain you give it and PUBLIC_URL to p9m.<domain> (https:// if certs/ already holds a certificate, else http://: run it again with the domain after adding one; a PUBLIC_URL you set yourself is kept), fills in random secrets, creates data/, opt/, certs/ and dynamic/, and prints the admin password and token. It keeps values you already set, so it is safe to run again. Without it: download env.example of the release as .env and set HOST_DOMAIN, PUBLIC_URL and the three secrets by hand.

docker compose up -d pulls the released image ghcr.io/csakaszamok/p9m. It carries the sandbox templates and runtimes, and the files the other services read: on every up the one-shot p9m-init service copies the Sablier themes, the error pages, the registry config and dynamic/errors.yml from it, so they always match the running version. To work on the code, see CONTRIBUTING.md.

The stack runs Traefik v3.6 with the Sablier plugin, Sablier, a registry and the Purgatorium API. The UI is at http://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN> (by default http://p9m.lvh.me, which resolves to 127.0.0.1), the API also on port 8081 of the host.

An app takes seconds to open the first time?

In Chrome, Settings → Privacy and security → Security → Use secure DNS: with "your current service provider" each new *.lvh.me name can wait for a slow or filtering resolver. Turn it off, or pick a provider such as Cloudflare (1.1.1.1).

Each sandbox's files (compose file, certificates, tunnel config) live in opt/sandboxes/<owner>/<name>/, its archives in opt/archive/<owner>/; <owner> is admin or the user's sign-in e-mail.

Give the Docker daemon a larger address pool. Every sandbox — sleeping ones included — keeps its own compose network until it is archived. Docker's default pools only allow about 30 networks; beyond that sandbox creation fails with fully subnetted. Set smaller subnets in the daemon config (/etc/docker/daemon.json, or Docker Desktop → Settings → Docker Engine) and restart Docker:

{ "default-address-pools": [ { "base": "10.64.0.0/12", "size": 28 } ] }

A sandbox network needs only a handful of addresses, so /28 subnets are enough: 10.64.0.0/12 holds 65536 of them (10.10.0.0/16 would hold 4096). Pick a range your server's own networks do not use (see ip route). Changing the pools later leaves the networks made before as they are: list the old pool too, after the new one, so Docker never hands out its addresses twice.

traefik-net is the exception: every running sandbox takes two addresses on it (its frps and socat), so on a /28 only 4 sandboxes can run at once, and the next one starts without its tunnel (no available IPv4 addresses on this network's address pools: traefik-net). Give it its own subnet, outside the pools above, in a docker-compose.override.yml next to docker-compose.yml (Docker Compose reads it on its own, and it stays when you replace docker-compose.yml on an upgrade):

networks:
  traefik-net:
    ipam:
      config:
        - subnet: 10.11.0.0/20

On a server already running, the network must be made again: take Purgatorium and the sandboxes' containers down (their data stays: they wake as from a deep sleep), remove the network, and start Purgatorium again:

docker compose down
for p in $(docker ps -a --format '{{.Label "com.docker.compose.project"}}' | sort -u | grep '^p9m-'); do docker compose -p "$p" down; done
docker network rm traefik-net
docker compose up -d

check-host.sh tells how many sandboxes traefik-net has room for.

Before exposing Purgatorium publicly, set ADMIN_TOKEN, SESSION_SECRET and ADMIN_PASSWORD to real secrets (setup.sh does). docker compose does not start without an ADMIN_TOKEN; the .env.example placeholders are only meant for local dev and the e2e scripts: Purgatorium logs a startup warning while one is in effect, and refuses to start with an https:// PUBLIC_URL. The direct API port 8081 listens on the host only (P9M_API_BIND), and OIDC needs OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS or OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS (see Configuration).

All settings: Configuration. For HTTPS: HTTPS.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
The same API is an MCP server at /mcp (Streamable HTTP): each endpoint is a tool, such as list_sandboxes, create_sandbox, wake_sandbox, sleep_sandbox, get_sandbox (with its app links), set_sleep_settings, and for the sandbox's files list_sandbox_files, read_sandbox_file, write_sandbox_file, create_sandbox_folder, delete_sandbox_file and list_sandbox_volumes (the apps' volumes, whose paths the other file tools take). A tool call runs the endpoint with the caller's token, so it can do exactly what that token can do on the REST API; a token limited to one sandbox stays limited to it, and is offered only the tools it may call (no create_sandbox, no token or SSH key management). Only tokens are accepted (not a browser session).

For Claude Code, add it by hand (the p9m plugin is a deploy skill and does not add it):

claude mcp add --transport http p9m https://p9m.example.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer p9m_…"

Other clients take the same URL and header, e.g. {"mcpServers": {"p9m": {"type": "http", "url": "https://p9m.example.com/mcp", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer p9m_…"}}}}. Left out: the log stream (it never ends) and the zip export (a file a tool result cannot carry).

A client that can only start a local process (stdio) can use scripts/mcp-stdio.mjs from this repository: it needs only Node.js 18+, no packages, and passes each message to the server's /mcp with your token:

{"mcpServers": {"p9m": {"command": "node", "args": ["/path/to/p9m/scripts/mcp-stdio.mjs"], "env": {"P9M_URL": "https://p9m.example.com", "P9M_TOKEN": "p9m_…"}}}}

Under the hood it is JSON-RPC over HTTP: one POST /mcp per call, no session to open first, so even curl can call a tool (tools/list, then tools/call with the tool's name and arguments):

docs.title: Isolation between sandboxes
docs.text:
An app in one sandbox must not reach another sandbox's apps. Today:

  • inner containers' private addresses are only reachable inside their own sandbox;
  • Sablier's API is on its own network (sablier-net) shared only with Traefik;
  • a sandbox container is on its own network only, with its frps and socat, so no other sandbox reaches it or its ports directly. Everything into it goes through its frp tunnel: its web addresses, its TLS TCP addresses, SSH and Docker access (frpc connects out of the sandbox to its frps, which is on traefik-net under the sandbox's name);
  • a port an inner container publishes on all interfaces (9000:9000) gets a link (its tunnel) and a TLS TCP address; a port published on 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1:9000:9000) is private to the sandbox: no link, no TCP address. A link whose app does not answer is marked ⚠ in the panel — usually the app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside its container; make it listen on 0.0.0.0.

The Purgatorium API itself requires authentication (see Web UI and sign-in). What a sandbox needs of Purgatorium's services it reaches through its own socat, under their usual names: the Docker Hub cache (registry-cache:5000), the registry and the UI (through Traefik). frps's own ports are high (65000 for frpc, 65080 for the web addresses, 65075 for its API, which has a per-sandbox password kept in frps.toml), because frps also listens on every port the sandbox publishes, and on 22 and 2376.

Who may open an app's web address can be limited per app with p9m.access (App access); that applies to HTTP through Purgatorium only, not to the TCP addresses below.

docs.title: App web addresses
docs.text:
Each TCP port an inner container publishes on all interfaces gets a web address, <sandbox>-<project>-<container>-port<host port>.<domain> (shop-inner-web-port8080.<domain>). A label on the container gives it a short one instead:

Label What it does p9m.subdomain: web The app's address becomes <sandbox>-web.<domain>. No other label does (p7y.subdomain and frpc.subdomain are ignored). shell gets no TCP address: that name is the sandbox's own SSH (Shell and logs). p9m.access Who may open the address (App access). p9m.connect.user The login the Connect… recipes use (below). p9m.publish, p9m.title, p9m.description, p9m.image Lists the app on the Hub. 
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    labels:
      p9m.subdomain: web

A container with p9m.subdomain that publishes several ports has one web address for all of them; each port's TCP address (below) gets -port<N> too.

docs.title: A separate domain for the apps
docs.text:
By default the apps are under HOST_DOMAIN, beside the UI. A server whose sandboxes run apps of people you do not fully trust should put them under a domain of their own, as GitHub Pages (github.io) and Vercel (vercel.app) do: set APPS_DOMAIN=example.app beside HOST_DOMAIN=example.dev.

  • What moves: every sandbox address, <sandbox>-<…>.example.app: the apps, the TCP and SSH addresses, Docker access. The UI, the registry and the Hub stay under example.dev.
  • Why: a phishing app reported to a blocklist (Google Safe Browsing, a company proxy) takes its domain with it; under its own domain, the UI and its sign-in stay reachable. To the browser, an app is then another site: it cannot set cookies for the UI's domain, nor send it same-site requests.
  • What it needs: a wildcard DNS record *.example.app pointing to the server, and the certificate covering *.example.app as well as *.example.dev (HTTPS: one certificate with both names).
  • The sandboxes made before: at the next start (docker compose up -d) Purgatorium moves them to the new domain, restarting those that run. Their old web addresses redirect to the new ones (308). A TCP, SSH or Docker client has to use the new address; Docker access needs its certificates made again (Docker access… says so).
  • The Public Suffix List: with the apps domain on the Public Suffix List (its private section; you request it), browsers and blocklists treat each app's address as a site of its own, so one bad app does not take the others with it. Purgatorium needs nothing for it: its app cookies are each app's own.

docs.title: TLS TCP addresses
docs.text:
A port an inner container publishes on all interfaces ("5432:5432") also gets a TCP address, its HTTP name plus -tcp, on port 443, TLS only: shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain>:443. Ports published on 127.0.0.1 stay private: no TCP address and no link.

  • Postgres: psql "host=shop-inner-db-port5432-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require …"
  • Any client that speaks TLS (Redis --tls, MQTTS): connect with that name as SNI.
  • SSH through TLS: ProxyCommand openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h.

Traefik passes these names through to Purgatorium's TCP gateway, which terminates TLS (with certs/tls.crt, or a self-signed *.<domain> kept in data/), wakes the sandbox if needed and connects to the sandbox's frps over traefik-net (the port's tcp proxy, through the tunnel to the sandbox). There is no extra authentication: the service's own login protects it. Only web traffic keeps a sandbox awake: without it the sandbox sleeps after its idle timeout even with an open TCP connection, which then drops; the next connection wakes it. Right after a wake the service itself may still be starting (Postgres answers the database system is starting up), so let the client retry. The details panel lists the addresses with ready-made commands (Connect…), picked by the container's own port (5432 Postgres, 6379 Redis, 22 or 2222 SSH; anything else gets the generic TLS recipe). A p9m.connect.user label on the container puts its login into those commands. The API gives the same as tcp_addresses (address, port, user) next to tcp_urls.

The tcp-demo template (on either runtime) shows it end to end. Its starter stack has a Postgres with a sample orders table (<name>-db-tcp), a Redis (<name>-redis-tcp), an SSH server with the user demo (<name>-ssh-tcp) and pgweb in the browser (https://<name>-pgweb.<domain>, user demo), all behind one generated password (Demo password in the details panel and in Connect…). Insert a row with psql and it shows up in pgweb:

psql "host=<name>-db-tcp.<domain> port=443 sslmode=require user=postgres dbname=postgres" -c "insert into orders (customer, item, amount) values ('me', 'espresso', 3)"
redis-cli -h <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -p 443 --tls --sni <name>-redis-tcp.<domain> -a <password> ping   # add --insecure with the self-signed certificate
ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" demo@<name>-ssh-tcp.<domain>

The three TCP containers also get an HTTP link in App ports (frpc tunnels every published port); those links do not lead anywhere useful.

docs.title: CPU and memory
docs.text:
Every sandbox runs with a CPU and memory limit: the sandbox and everything inside it share it (the inner containers live in the sandbox container's cgroup). New sandboxes get SANDBOX_CPUS / SANDBOX_MEMORY (default 2 CPUs, 4 GB); on create (Advanced) or later (Resources… in the panel, PATCH /sandboxes/:name with cpus, memory) a user can raise their sandbox's limits up to SANDBOX_MAX_CPUS / SANDBOX_MAX_MEMORY (default 4 and 8 GB), the admin up to the host's size. A change applies at once without a restart (docker update) and is kept in the sandbox's compose file. Memory below what a running sandbox uses now is refused (stop it first). There is no swap beyond the memory limit.

The panel shows the sandbox's current CPU and memory against its limits (sampled every 10 s), and the list a short CPU · Mem column for running sandboxes. The API gives limits (cpus, memory in bytes) and, for a running sandbox, usage (cpu in cores, memory, memory_limit).

docs.title: Disk
docs.text:
Everything a sandbox keeps (its inner images, containers and volumes) is in its own docker_data volume. Purgatorium measures it from outside with du: a running sandbox every 15 minutes, an asleep one once after it stopped (its size does not change while it sleeps); the results are kept in data/disk-usage.json. The Resources tab shows the use against the sandbox's disk limit, SANDBOX_DISK (20 GB by default); the admin can set another one per sandbox (Change limits…, or PATCH /sandboxes/:name with disk).

Above the limit the panel and the sandbox list show ⚠ and suggest cleaning up (docker system prune in the sandbox). It is only a warning: nothing is stopped or refused, and a sandbox can use more until the host's disk is full. A hard limit (a fixed-size disk per sandbox) is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Open, not yet scheduled
docs.text:
• A Kata Containers runtime, for untrusted code. Each sandbox in its own lightweight VM with its own kernel, so root inside a sandbox no longer means root on the host (today's dind runtime is privileged). Docker supports Kata through its containerd shim ("runtimes": {"kata": {"runtimeType": "io.containerd.kata.v2"}} in the host's daemon.json, then runtime: kata in the sandbox's compose service), so it fits next to dind and sysbox as a third runtime with the same wiring (FRP tunnel, Traefik route, Sablier, docker_data volume, archive). To work out:
  • the host needs hardware virtualization (KVM): bare metal, or a cloud VM with nested virtualization;
  • dockerd inside the Kata VM: privileged there applies to the VM only, not the host, but must not pass the host's devices through;
  • the docker_data volume and its performance (virtio-fs), and how the CPU and memory limits map to the VM's size;
  • a foxglove image for it, and the same integration tests as for the other runtimes;
  • still a sandbox (same API, lifecycle, quota and UI), with its isolation shown as a badge next to its name and chosen at create time ("Isolation: Container / MicroVM"): dind 🟠 privileged, sysbox 🔵 container, kata 🟢 microVM. "MicroVM" is said only where it is true: dind and sysbox sandboxes share the host's kernel.
  • GPUs in sandboxes. Today no sandbox sees a GPU. A sandbox could ask for one at create time, like CPUs and memory, and the list, the panel and the API would show which have one (a GPU column with the model, e.g. RTX 4090). It suits the sleep model: a sleeping sandbox could give its GPU back, and the next one to wake take it. To work out:
  • per runtime: dind needs the NVIDIA driver and nvidia-container-toolkit on the host, the device passed to the sandbox container and the toolkit in the foxglove image, so the inner Docker hands it on to the apps; whether and how sysbox (the production runtime) passes GPUs through, to check first; Kata only through VFIO, typically one GPU per VM;
  • detecting the host's GPUs at startup and in check-host.sh (nvidia-smi, Docker's runtimes);
  • limits and quota (SANDBOX_MAX_GPUS, the admin beyond), as for CPU and memory;
  • a whole GPU per sandbox, or shared (time-slicing, MIG);
  • what a waking sandbox does when every GPU is taken: wait, refuse, or start without one.
  • Every path into a sandbox through frp, next steps. Since 0.12.23 every path goes through the frp tunnel: web addresses (Traefik → <name>-socat:8080 → frps), and the TLS TCP addresses, Docker access and SSH (Traefik → Purgatorium's TCP gateway → the sandbox's frps on traefik-net, frpc's tcp proxies). frpc connects out of the sandbox, so the same wiring can carry sandboxes whose inside is not directly reachable: a microVM runtime (Kata, Firecracker), sandboxes on another machine or behind NAT, Kubernetes pods. Still open:
  • the TCP path still needs Purgatorium (its addresses do not answer while Purgatorium is down or upgrading, and open connections drop): whether Traefik could carry it with TCP routers to frps, which have no Sablier middleware;
  • one rule for staying awake on every path: traffic in the last minute, not an open connection (today: every web request; a -docker connection while bytes go through it, never waking a sleeping one, since Docker Desktop reconnects to every context at once; a -tcp connection not at all, though it wakes one);
  • sandboxes that are meant to talk to each other (one's app using another's database) do it through the TLS TCP addresses; an opt-in shared network is not there.
  • The Hub, next steps. The Hub lists the apps builders publish with a label. Still open: a webhook when an app is published (Slack, n8n, a Lemmy bot, without an RSS reader in between); a Hub per team, with Teams; a Hub open on the internal network without signing in, for small installs without single sign-on; p9m.publish.port to choose which of an app's ports it opens.
  • Deploy from git. Today a sandbox gets its apps through docker compose (the API, SSH, the Docker CLI or an agent). Next: connect a repository, and a push builds the image and deploys it into the sandbox, like a self-hosted Vercel; optionally a preview sandbox per branch or pull request, which sleeps like any other and is archived when the branch is merged. To work out:
  • where the build runs: in the sandbox's own Docker (its CPU and memory limits apply, and the image goes to the Purgatorium registry, which already scans pushes for secrets);
  • how Purgatorium reaches the repository and hears about pushes: a webhook from GitHub/GitLab/Gitea, or polling, and a deploy key per sandbox;
  • projects without a Dockerfile or a compose file: buildpacks (Nixpacks, Cloud Native Buildpacks), or refuse them with a clear message;
  • build logs in the panel and the API, and what a failed build does to the running version (it keeps running).
  • Coding agents inside a sandbox. Today the agent runs on the user's machine and drives a sandbox from outside (a token for that sandbox and its Docker keys in the project's .p9m folder). Next: the agent itself runs in a sandbox, like Docker Sandboxes (sbx) on a laptop, but on the team's server: it works next to its apps, and what it builds is at a URL for colleagues at once, which neither Coder (a workspace for writing code) nor an SDK sandbox gives. To work out:
  • an agent image: a foxglove variant with Claude Code, Node, uv and gh (not Docker's sandbox-templates image, which has no dockerd TLS listener, frpc or sshd), as a runtime next to sysbox; the user signs in over SSH at first;
  • sleep: a sandbox now sleeps after idle_timeout without web traffic, so a working agent would be stopped; an agent session must count as activity (a heartbeat, or a watch on its SSH / tmux session);
  • secrets outside the sandbox: an egress sidecar in the runtime's compose file, the sandbox's own network internal: true, and the model's key (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL pointing at the sidecar) and a GitHub token (url.<sidecar>.insteadOf) added by the sidecar, so the agent never sees them; a per-user secret store in Purgatorium to fill them from; a domain allowlist for the rest of its traffic (the egress rules missing today);
  • starting and following a session from the UI: a web terminal, or Claude Code's remote control.
  • Teams: a sandbox owned by a group, so several people see and manage it, and other teams do not; optionally a quota per team.
  • A hard disk quota per sandbox. Today a sandbox above its disk limit is only flagged (see Disk). For a hard limit: its docker_data as a fixed-size ext4 image, loop-mounted through the local volume driver (type=ext4, o=loop); to work out: moving existing sandboxes' data, resizing (only while stopped), the archive, Docker Desktop. The Kata runtime gets this from its VM disk.
  • Kubernetes support: move the runtime layer behind the Docker-specific code; Sablier's Kubernetes provider helps here.

docs.title: Runtimes and templates
docs.text:
A sandbox is a runtime (how it runs) plus a template (what runs inside), picked separately on create (runtime, template; the New sandbox form has a select for each):

Runtime Isolation Use sysbox runtime: sysbox-runc, no privileged mode every server (the only one allowed by default); requires sysbox on a Linux host dind privileged: true development only (a laptop, Docker Desktop / WSL, where sysbox cannot run): root in a dind sandbox can reach the host. Never on a server; allowed only with ALLOWED_RUNTIMES=sysbox,dind (or all) Template What runs inside starter (default) a hello app; deploy yours with docker, SSH or an agent portainer the same with Portainer, a web UI for the sandbox's Docker (its address and password in the API and the panel; it runs with -H unix:///var/run/docker.sock, so its environment exists from the start) claude-code Claude Code in Docker Sandboxes' (sbx) image, docker/sandbox-templates:claude-code, next to the sandbox's own Docker, and a hello app: open the sandbox's terminal in the claude container and run claude; it builds and runs with docker compose, and what it publishes gets an address. Its home directory is a volume (the sign-in and ~/workspace survive sleep). The image is large: about 5 GB of disk per sandbox claude-code-minimal the same, slim: ghcr.io/csakaszamok/p9m-claude-code-minimal (built from images/claude-code-minimal with every release) has Claude Code, the Docker CLI with compose and buildx, git and little else, about 1.5 GB of disk per sandbox. The agent builds and runs the apps in containers, so it needs no toolchains of its own claude-code-ecc the slim one with ECC installed into Claude Code as the ecc@ecc plugin (pinned to a release): agents, skills and hooks for a plan → test → review workflow, Node.js and Python for its hooks. For trying ECC out: it adds about 31k tokens of context to every session, and its gate asks Claude to state the request before the first shell command of a session. ghcr.io/csakaszamok/p9m-claude-code-ecc, built from images/claude-code-ecc with every release; about 2 GB of disk per sandbox tcp-demo a demo of TLS TCP addresses: Postgres, Redis, SSH and pgweb empty nothing: no starter stack; deploy your apps afterwards

Both runtimes have the same wiring (FRP tunnel, Traefik route, Sablier sleep/wake, docker_data volume, archive on delete). The sysbox image runs plain dockerd, so its TLS listener is configured through the runtime's daemon_json field, which Purgatorium merges into the generated daemon.json. Only sysbox belongs on a server, and it is the only runtime allowed unless ALLOWED_RUNTIMES says otherwise (see Security).

Runtimes are runtimes/<name>.yaml: a description, the sandbox's own docker_compose (the DinD container, frps, socat, and their Traefik and Sablier labels) and an optional daemon_json. Templates are directories, templates/<name>/:

  • compose.yaml (required): the stack deployed into the sandbox's own Docker on creation, a plain compose file.
  • template.yaml (optional, every field optional): description (default: the directory name), before_script (JavaScript run on create; what it returns becomes ${variables} for both compose files and the sandbox's extras, e.g. a generated password), idle_timeout (Go duration, default 30m: how long a sandbox may go without HTTP traffic before it sleeps; a create request can override it), deep_sleep_after (default 7d), inner_project_name (default inner).

A new template is a new directory; it shows up in GET /templates and the form without a restart. In both files Purgatorium fills in ${name}, ${raw_name}, ${host_domain} (the domain of the sandbox's addresses: APPS_DOMAIN, or HOST_DOMAIN without it), ${template_name}, ${runtime_name} and whatever before_script returned; any other ${…} is left for docker compose (write $$ for a literal $). Publish a port on all interfaces ("5432:5432") to give it a link and a TLS TCP address; a port on 127.0.0.1 stays private to the sandbox; a p9m.connect.user label puts its login into the Connect… commands. Pass passwords through variables whose name contains PASSWORD (or TOKEN, SECRET, KEY): Starter stack… masks those.

A template is only the start. The New sandbox dialog shows the chosen template's starter stack, read-only: a sandbox starts with it as it is, and it cannot be changed, neither at the create (the API refuses a compose text) nor later. Your own apps, Claude Code added to a sandbox made from starter, anything else, go in afterwards like every app: through the sandbox's Docker, with docker, SSH or an agent (Purgatorium for agents). Sandboxes created from an edited compose text before 0.17 keep it and still show "(edited)". docker compose runs in the sandbox itself, on the sandbox's own Docker, with the file at /inner/docker-compose.yml: whatever the file makes it read, build or run (build, env_file, include, secrets from a file…) is the sandbox's, never the Purgatorium server's. build contexts and other relative paths are under /inner. The CLI gets an empty environment, so an unknown ${VAR} is empty.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Purgatorium is built for a team that trusts each other's intentions but not each other's mistakes: it keeps one person's broken compose file, runaway container or exposed port from affecting everyone else. It is not a boundary against hostile code.

What it does:

  • each user gets their own Docker daemon, so their containers, images, volumes and networks are separate from everyone else's and from the host's Docker;
  • an app's private addresses are reachable only inside its own sandbox, and ports published on 127.0.0.1 only through its tunnel (see Isolation between sandboxes);
  • users see and change only their own sandboxes, through the UI, the API or a personal access token; the admin sees all;
  • a sandbox's web apps open only for its owner (and the admin) unless labelled domain or public (App access);
  • with an https:// PUBLIC_URL, Purgatorium refuses to start with default secrets; docker compose does not start without an ADMIN_TOKEN, and Purgatorium does not start with OIDC open to anyone (OIDC_ALLOW_ANYONE=true aside);
  • the direct plain-HTTP API port 8081 listens on the host only (P9M_API_BIND): from elsewhere everything goes through Traefik.

On every server: install sysbox on the host. Only sysbox is allowed by default (ALLOWED_RUNTIMES), so nobody can create a privileged dind sandbox; without sysbox no sandbox can be created at all. The dind runtime is for development only (a laptop, Docker Desktop): never allow it on a server. check-host.sh tells whether sysbox works on the machine, and, run in the p9m folder, lists what else is not secure. Sandboxes that already exist keep their runtime: recreate the dind ones.

What it does not do:

  • Without sysbox, sandboxes run privileged (the dind runtime). Code with root inside such a sandbox can escape to the host. That is why only sysbox is allowed by default, which runs Docker in an unprivileged container; Docker Desktop cannot run sysbox, so for development there dind is allowed (docker-compose.dev.yml), and Purgatorium says so at startup. Only let people and agents you would give a shell on the host run code in dind sandboxes.
  • sysbox is not a VM: its sandboxes run unprivileged, in their own user namespace, but share the host's kernel, so a kernel exploit would still reach the host.
  • There is no network policy between a sandbox and the internet, and no hard disk quota per sandbox: only a warning above its disk limit (see Disk); CPU and memory limits exist (see CPU and memory).
  • The Purgatorium container mounts the host's Docker socket, so whoever controls Purgatorium controls the host. That is why a sandbox's starter stack is always its template's (no compose text of the user's goes through Purgatorium), and is run by docker compose inside the sandbox, not in the Purgatorium container; why the files Purgatorium reads and writes in a sandbox's directory are mounted into the sandbox read-only (/inner, and of /certs only its dockerd's certificate), and read and written without following a symlink; and why Purgatorium's internal port (app access for Traefik) listens only on a network no sandbox is on. Traefik's API is not served.
  • A sandbox is on its own network only: Purgatorium and Traefik reach it through its frp tunnel (frpc connects out of it), so no sandbox reaches another one's ports past app access.
  • A host folder the admin mounts into a sandbox (HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS) is the sandbox owner's, as root, and every app's and agent's in it: read-only only limits writing. Keep the roots narrow.

In short, run it for a team, on a server you can rebuild, best behind a VPN or with the sign-in limited to your domain; for untrusted code (public sign-up, code from strangers), use a microVM-based sandbox instead; a Kata Containers runtime (a VM per sandbox) is on the roadmap.

Found a vulnerability? See SECURITY.md.

docs.title: SSH into a sandbox
docs.text:
Every sandbox runs an sshd: root, keys only, at <name>-shell-tcp.<domain>:443 (the same TLS gateway as the TCP addresses). Add your public keys under My area → SSH keys (/settings/ssh-keys, API GET/POST/DELETE /ssh-keys): they let you into all your sandboxes, and a change takes effect at once. A create request can add keys for that sandbox only (ssh_keys, or Advanced → Extra SSH public keys). Inside, docker talks to the sandbox's own Docker.

ssh -o ProxyCommand="openssl s_client -quiet -connect %h:443 -servername %h" root@<name>-shell-tcp.<domain>

Each new sandbox also has a key of its own: Download key in its panel (API GET /sandboxes/:name/ssh-key; POST makes one for an SSH sandbox that has none yet), so nobody has to make or upload a key first. The Connect… recipe then reads ssh -i ~/Downloads/<name>.key ….

The name shell is reserved: an inner service with p9m.subdomain: shell gets no TCP address.

docs.title: Terminal in the browser
docs.text: Terminal in a sandbox's panel opens a root shell in the sandbox in a new tab: nothing to install, no key. It wakes the sandbox if it is asleep, and keeps it awake while the tab is open. Inside, docker talks to the sandbox's own Docker. Only the sandbox's owner (and the admin) can open it, from the Purgatorium pages themselves (signed in; not with a token); at most 5 at once per user.

docs.title: Terminal in a container
docs.text: The Containers tab of a sandbox's panel (not in Simple) lists the containers in the sandbox's own Docker: name, compose project and service, image, state (API GET /sandboxes/:name/containers). Terminal next to a running one opens the same browser terminal, in that container: as the container's own user (its user:), in its working directory, with that user's login shell (else bash, else sh). That is the way into an app that only has a console, e.g. Claude Code in a devcontainer. The rules are the terminal's above; closing the tab ends the shell and what runs in it (Claude Code keeps its conversations: claude --continue picks up again; or run it in tmux).

docs.title: App logs
docs.text: Logs in a sandbox's panel opens, in a new tab, what the apps in the sandbox write: the last 100 lines of every container (time, service name; errors in red), then new lines as they come. A filter shows one service; Pause holds new lines, Clear empties the view. It does not wake the sandbox or keep it awake: a sleeping one says asleep with a Start button. With a token: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://p9m.example.com/sandboxes/p9m-shop/logs/stream. At most 5 viewers per sandbox at once.

docs.title: Sleep and wake
docs.text:
A sandbox is running, asleep (containers stopped, data intact), in deep sleep (containers and network removed, data intact) or archived (after an explicit delete). There is no fixed-time expiry: a sandbox only sleeps when nobody uses it, and only a person deleting it removes it.

Handled entirely by Sablier. The sandbox's outer containers (DinD, frps, socat) form one Sablier group and its Traefik router carries the Sablier middleware. After idle_timeout without HTTP traffic the group is stopped — which stops everything inside the sandbox too. The sandbox's router exists only while it runs, so the next request reaches Purgatorium's catch-all /wake, which wakes it within the owner's limits (see Web UI and sign-in) and shows a waiting page until the router is back; the socat healthcheck only passes once the FRP tunnel is online (an app's HTTP proxy, or for a stack that publishes no port, frpc's readiness marker for 15 seconds). Sablier still measures the idle time and puts the sandbox to sleep. Reset next to Sleeps in in the panel (POST /sandboxes/:name/keep-awake) starts the countdown over, as a visit would; it does not wake a sleeping sandbox.

Apps must set a restart policy to come back after sleep. When the sandbox wakes, its inner Docker daemon only restarts containers with restart: unless-stopped or restart: always. Without one, the app stays stopped and has to be started by hand (docker start, or from Portainer):

services:
  web:
    image: my-app
    restart: unless-stopped
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    restart: unless-stopped

HTTP traffic through Traefik counts as activity, and so does traffic on a Docker connection (DOCKER_HOST=tcp://<raw>-docker.<domain>:443): Purgatorium renews the session once a minute while bytes go through it. A Docker connection that is only open does not count, and a Docker connection never wakes a sleeping sandbox: Docker Desktop keeps every context connected for its Builds view and reconnects at once, so it would wake the sandbox each time it fell asleep. Wake it first (Wake, POST /sandboxes/:name/start, or open one of its apps); until then docker cannot connect. Sablier persists its sessions (--storage.file), so restarting Sablier does not put running sandboxes to sleep. A sandbox started without Purgatorium (Docker restarting it, docker compose start by hand, or Purgatorium restarted while it was starting one) has no session at first; Purgatorium notices within two minutes and opens one, so it still sleeps after its idle_timeout. After a host reboot, sandboxes that were asleep stay asleep.

The sandbox list (GET /sandboxes adds stops_at, deep_sleep_at and deep_sleep_after to each row) and the details panel show Sleeps in (time until Sablier stops a running sandbox; every request resets it — read from Sablier's /metrics, which Purgatorium reaches on sablier-net) and Deep sleep in (time until an asleep sandbox is taken down).

Both times can be changed after creation — Change… next to Sleep on the panel's Details tab, or PATCH /sandboxes/<name> with {"idle_timeout": "45m", "deep_sleep_after": "14d"} (either field; same formats as at creation; owner or admin). The values are written into the sandbox's docker-compose.yml. A new idle_timeout recreates only the socat container, which carries the Sablier middleware labels: a running sandbox's apps are unreachable for a few seconds, an asleep one stays asleep, and the DinD container and its inner stack are not touched; it applies from the next request's Sablier session. A new deep_sleep_after applies immediately — Purgatorium reads it from the compose file.

idle_timeout takes seconds, minutes, hours or days (30s, 30m, 2h, 1d); days are kept as hours (1d becomes 24h), because Sablier's durations have no days. deep_sleep_after takes m, h or d. The server can set a ceiling for users' sandboxes: SANDBOX_MAX_IDLE_TIMEOUT and SANDBOX_MAX_DEEP_SLEEP_AFTER (Configuration); a value above it, or never, is refused (at most 2h on this server). 0 or off means never, for both — at creation and when changing them. deep_sleep_after: off never takes the sandbox down. Sablier has no "never", so idle_timeout: off is written as a 10-year session (87600h): the sandbox keeps running, and if it is stopped by hand the next request still wakes it. The panel and the list show "never" for either.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
To a new version, in the install directory:

curl -fsSLO https://github.com/csakaszamok/p9m/releases/latest/download/docker-compose.yml
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d

If .env sets P9M_VERSION, change or remove it. Each release's notes are in the changelog.

docs.title: To 0.14.0: the secure defaults
docs.text:
Purgatorium 0.14.0 no longer starts with open defaults. Before docker compose up -d, check .env:

  • ADMIN_TOKEN must be set: docker compose refuses to start without it (the compose file had abc123 as a fallback). ./setup.sh fills in a random one; scripts and agents using the old token need the new one.
  • The API port 8081 listens on the host only. If something on another machine called http://<server>:8081 (a script, or docker clients getting registry tokens while PUBLIC_URL is empty), point it at PUBLIC_URL instead, or set P9M_API_BIND=0.0.0.0 on a trusted network.
  • With OIDC on, set OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS or OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS, or Purgatorium refuses to start (docker compose logs p9m says why). To keep letting anyone with an account at the provider in, set OIDC_ALLOW_ANYONE=true.

./check-host.sh, run in the install directory, lists what is still open.

docs.title: From Purgatory (p7y)
docs.text: There is no upgrade from Purgatory (p7y), the project's former name: install Purgatorium afresh, in a new directory called p9m. Nothing is carried over: sandboxes, archives, users, tokens and settings start empty, and P7Y_* settings and p7y.* labels are not read.

docs.title: Web UI and sign-in
docs.text:
Purgatorium has a small web UI (http://p9m.<HOST_DOMAIN>, or UI_HOST) for creating and managing sandboxes without the API directly, alongside the REST API.

Only the admin

Users have no web UI: they get and use their sandboxes from Claude Code (/p9m:init). A user who signs in sees only how to install the plugin; the sign-in is for approving /p9m:init (and for apps open only to signed-in people, see App access). A user's sign-in reaches no API either: users work with tokens. What follows is the admin's UI.

The users have an address of their own, sbx.<HOST_DOMAIN> by default (USER_HOST, see Configuration): they sign in and approve /p9m:init there, and UI_HOST is the admin's only.

Two ways to sign in:

  • Admin: a local account, set via ADMIN_USER / ADMIN_PASSWORD. Signs in with the "Administrator sign-in" form, which is there only with ADMIN_LOGIN=on (off by default: for emergencies), and sees every sandbox (My area + All sandboxes). Everyday, the admin signs in with OIDC, from an address in OIDC_ADMIN_EMAILS.
  • Signed out for doing nothing: after 30 minutes without a click, a key or a scroll (SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT), with a warning two minutes before; the header shows the time left next to the user's name; the automatic refreshes of the list do not count, so a tab left open does not stay signed in.
  • Against guessing: an address with 5 failed admin password sign-ins within 15 minutes has to wait 1 minute, then 2, 4… up to an hour after each further failure; after 30 failed admin passwords in an hour from all addresses together, the admin password is refused for everyone until the hour is over (OIDC still works). Failed OIDC sign-ins are only logged, never counted: a callback cannot be guessed, and a room behind one address (a workshop, an office) would lock itself out with a few wrong accounts. Every refusal is logged as [login] <address>: …, e.g. for fail2ban. The address is the one Traefik saw; the counts are kept in memory (a restart forgets them).
  • Everyone else: OIDC (Google or any OpenID Connect provider). Configure OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET and register the redirect URI $PUBLIC_URL/auth/callback (and the users' address's, https://<USER_HOST>/auth/callback, by default https://sbx.<HOST_DOMAIN>/auth/callback, too) with the provider — character for character (scheme, no trailing slash), under Google's Authorized redirect URIs, otherwise sign-in fails with redirect_uri_mismatch. Google accepts http:// redirect URIs only for localhost, so with Google use an https:// PUBLIC_URL (locally: a self-signed *.lvh.me certificate in certs/ and PUBLIC_URL=https://p9m.lvh.me, see HTTPS). OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME labels the sign-in button (default Google). Signed-in users only see their own sandboxes.

SESSION_SECRET signs the session cookie — set it to a long random string; sessions issued under an old value stop working if it changes.

OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS or OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS says who may sign in and create sandboxes (e.g. example.com): with OIDC on, Purgatorium refuses to start without one of them, since with Google any Google account would get in. OIDC_ALLOW_ANYONE=true lets anyone with an account at the provider in, if that is what you want. An account not on the list is told so on the sign-in page; one taken off the list is signed out, and its tokens stop working, once Purgatorium restarts with the new list. Each user may have SANDBOX_QUOTA sandboxes running at once (default 3, 0 = unlimited), guaranteed, and with SANDBOX_QUOTA_MAX more while the server has room to spare for the others' guarantees (Running 4 / 3 · up to 10 beside New sandbox); asleep, deep-sleeping and archived ones are not counted, so letting a sandbox sleep frees its place, and the admin is not limited. At the limit a user can neither create a sandbox nor wake one, from sleep or deep sleep: its address shows Running limit reached, its address shows Running limit reached with the running sandboxes, and Wake in the panel lets the owner put one to sleep instead (POST /sandboxes/:name/start with {"sleep": "<name>"}). Purgatorium never puts a sandbox to sleep on its own. Running sandboxes' web addresses do not go through Purgatorium: they keep working while it is down; waking needs it, and so do the TLS TCP addresses and Docker access (they go through Purgatorium's TCP gateway). SANDBOX_MAX_TOTAL (default 200) caps the running sandboxes on the whole server, the admin's included (asleep ones take no place): when it is reached nobody but the admin can create one or wake one (The server is full). The sign-in page shows the sandbox places above the sign-in buttons (taken and free; LOGIN_CAPACITY=off hides them), and once signed in the top bar does, on every page (e.g. 142 / 200 places, the free ones on hover; orange from 90%, red when full). The Overview page shows the counts as cards: running of how many allowed, asleep, deep sleep and archived; for the admin the sandbox places used against the server limit (the admin's own sandboxes take places too), the host's CPU and memory (used now and reserved by running sandboxes), the disk use, a table per owner and a Users table. Users lists every account that has signed in (by e-mail; admin for the local admin): when it was last seen (a page load, at most every 10 minutes), its last sign-in and how many, its sandboxes now and created, and its last API use (its tokens); no sandbox yet marks someone who signed in but never created one. The rows are kept in data/user-stats.json until the admin deletes one (Delete: only the row; the account and its sandboxes stay). Only the admin sees them (GET /users, DELETE /users/:account).

Users get their tokens from Claude Code: each /p9m:init approval makes one for that sandbox only, valid 90 days, in the project's .p9m folder. From My area → Access tokens (/settings/tokens), the admin can mint a personal access token (p9m_…) for agents to use as Authorization: Bearer p9m_…; the token acts as the admin for the API. The full token is shown once, at creation. Tokens can be set to expire in 30 days, 90 days, or never. The page lists every account's tokens, and the admin can revoke any of them, e.g. one a user lost: users cannot.

A token can also be limited to one sandbox (Access in the dialog, or Token for this sandbox… on a sandbox panel's Access tab). Such a token lists and opens only that sandbox, and can start, stop and restart it and change its sleep times; it cannot create or delete sandboxes or manage tokens (403), and any other sandbox answers 404. Deleting the sandbox leaves the token in place: if you restore the sandbox, it works again.

With such a token an agent can deploy and update apps in the user's sandbox: the Purgatorium API gives it the sandbox's Docker client certificates, and the docker command line reaches the sandbox's own Docker daemon (or, in a sandbox from the portainer template, the Portainer API). Step by step: agent guide.

docs.title: Simple and Advanced
docs.text: The top bar has a Simple | Advanced switch, remembered for the admin (starting in Advanced). Simple is for when you only want apps online: the menu shows My area only (your sandboxes, without its tabs); the list shows the name, status, Sleeps in and age; a new sandbox asks for a name and a template; a sandbox panel has Wake or Sleep, an App ports tab (the web address of each app and Let your agent deploy…: the Claude Code plugin or a zip for other agents, the same window as in Advanced, which adds its Options) and a Details tab (when it last ran, the sleep times, warnings, archiving). Advanced shows everything: Overview, tokens, SSH keys, the Terminal and Logs, and the Containers, Access, Files, Resources and Registry tabs. Simple only hides: what an account may do is the same in both, and the API and MCP do not change. PUT /me/view with {"view": "simple"} or {"view": "advanced"} sets it; GET /me returns it as view, and whether the account may switch as view_switch.

docs.title: Light and dark
docs.text: The pages follow the device's light or dark setting until the account chooses one with the sun / moon button in the top bar; the choice is remembered for the account, so it holds on any computer. The sign-in page, before anyone is signed in, always follows the device. The page shown while a sandbox wakes up, the error pages, the terminal and the log view stay dark. PUT /me/theme with {"theme": "light"}, "dark" or "system" sets it; GET /me returns it as theme (null: the device decides).

docs.title: Host folders
docs.text:
The admin can mount folders of the host into a sandbox, e.g. a shared data folder, when HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS lists where they may come from (e.g. HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS=/srv/shared; see Configuration). On a sandbox panel's Resources tab, Host folders lists them, with Remove for each, and a form to add one: the host folder (at or under one of the roots), where it appears in the sandbox (empty: /mnt/<last part of the host path>) and read-only. The folder is bind-mounted into the sandbox container, so the apps in the sandbox's own Docker can bind it from there too (e.g. /mnt/shared:/data).

Adding or removing one recreates the sandbox container, after a confirmation: a running sandbox restarts (its apps are unreachable for a few seconds), an asleep one stays asleep, one in deep sleep gets the change when it wakes. A host folder that does not exist is not created: Docker refuses it, the panel shows Docker's message and nothing changes. The target cannot be /, a system directory (/etc, /usr, /proc, /dev, /run…) or on, above or under one of the sandbox's own mounts (/var/lib/docker, /opt, /root, /home, /srv, …). The mounts are kept in the sandbox's compose file (and its p9m.mounts label), so they survive sleep, deep sleep and upgrades.

A mount gives whoever owns the sandbox that host folder, as root, and every app and agent in it: mount read-only what they need not change, and only what they may see. The owner can list them through the API (GET /sandboxes/:name/mounts); only the admin adds or removes them, on the Resources tab (in Simple, Details lists them). With HOST_MOUNT_ROOTS unset no mount can be added; ones already there stay until the admin removes them. API: GET, POST and DELETE /sandboxes/:name/mounts (see API), over MCP list_sandbox_mounts, add_sandbox_mount and remove_sandbox_mount.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Step by step, from nothing to an app with a link you can send to anyone. No server knowledge needed: your coding agent does the technical part.

  • Put your app online with Claude Code: install the p9m plugin once, approve each project in the browser, then say deploy this app. The easiest way.
  • Put your app online with any agent: Codex, Cursor, or Claude Code without the plugin, with the .p9m folder Claude Code makes once, or a zip from the admin.
  • Share your app with your team on the Hub: list it where colleagues find, open and vote for it.

You need a Purgatorium account: the address your team uses (for example https://p9m.example.com) and a sign-in. Someone in your team set Purgatorium up; to set up your own, see Install.

docs.title: Put your app online with Claude Code
docs.text:
You have an app on your computer (a website, a dashboard, a small tool) and you want a link to it that works for anyone. Claude Code builds and runs it in your Purgatorium sandbox and gives you that link.

What you need: Claude Code (in a terminal, or the Code tab of the Claude desktop app), Docker installed on your computer, and a Purgatorium account.

docs.title: 1. Install the p9m plugin in Claude Code (once)
docs.text:
Open a terminal (in VS Code: Terminal → New Terminal; on Windows also PowerShell, on a Mac the Terminal app), paste these two lines one after the other and press Enter after each:

claude plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m

It installs the plugin for you, in all your projects. It asks for no address and no token. Purgatorium shows these lines too, once you sign in at its address.

Good to know

  • claude not found? Claude Code is not installed for the terminal: see Claude Code's setup. An unknown option means an older Claude Code: run claude update.
  • Already in Claude Code? The same two lines there are /plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m and /plugin install p9m@p9m. (The Claude Code panel in VS Code has no /plugin: use the terminal.)

You install the plugin once. Each project then gets its sandbox in the next step.

docs.title: 2. Get a sandbox for your project folder (once per folder)
docs.text:
A sandbox is your own small server: your app runs there, not on your computer. You get it from Claude Code; Purgatorium's web page is only for approving.

  1. Open your app's folder in Claude Code: start claude in that folder, or open the folder in VS Code or the desktop app.

  2. Type this into Claude Code, with your Purgatorium's address, and press Enter:

    /p9m:init https://p9m.example.com

  3. Claude Code answers with a link and a code, for example:

    Open https://p9m.example.com/activate?code=TGMH-BSGQ and approve the code TGMH-BSGQ.

  4. Open the link in your browser and sign in. The page shows the code and what Claude Code asks for: a new sandbox. Check that the code is the same one Claude Code printed, then click Create and approve. Creating it takes up to a minute.

  5. The page then shows another code, for example KPRW-DMXT. Copy it, paste it into Claude Code and press Enter. Claude Code says the folder is connected, and the sandbox's name (like k3x9q2). That is all.

Approve only your own code

Approve a code only if you just ran /p9m:init yourself and Claude Code shows that same code. If someone sends you a link like this, do not approve it, and never give anyone the code the page shows after Approve: whoever has it gets into your sandbox. Click Deny instead.

What happened behind the scenes: Claude Code got a token for this one sandbox and the sandbox's Docker keys, and wrote them into a .p9m folder in your project. You never see or copy them. The folder is secret, and it keeps itself out of git on its own: leave it there. The token works for 90 days (then run /p9m:init again with the sandbox's name, see below).

If something goes wrong

  • The code ran out: it works for 10 minutes and only once. Run the same /p9m:init line again for a new code.
  • You clicked Deny by mistake: run /p9m:init again.
  • A wrong code pasted: Claude Code asks again; after 5 wrong ones, run /p9m:init again.
  • The sandbox could not be created: the page says why, often that you have as many sandboxes running as you may. Let one sleep (let my other sandbox sleep, in its project folder) and click Create and approve again.
  • The folder was connected to another sandbox already: Claude Code asks before it replaces that connection.

docs.title: 3. Deploy
docs.text:
In the same folder, say in your own words:

Deploy this app.

Claude Code wakes the sandbox, builds your app there, starts it and checks that it answers. At the end it gives you a link like https://shop-web.example.com (your sandbox's name first). Open it: that is your app, and it works for anyone you send it to.

docs.title: 4. Change and update
docs.text:
Changed something? Say:

Update the app.

The same link shows the new version a few seconds later.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Sleep: when nobody uses the app for a while (30 minutes by default), the sandbox sleeps to free the server. The next visit wakes it in a few seconds: the visitor sees waking up and then your app. Nothing is lost.
  • Sleep later: let it sleep only after 2 hours without visitors works too (never sleep as well).
  • It does not answer? Ask Claude Code why does my app not answer?: it reads the app's logs in the sandbox. The usual cause is an app that listens only on localhost; Claude Code fixes that.
  • Only for you or your colleagues? Say make it visible only to me (or only to my colleagues): Claude Code sets p9m.access (App access), and opening the link then asks the visitor to sign in to Purgatorium.
  • Docker is needed on your computer only for its command line: the build runs in the sandbox.

docs.title: More projects
docs.text:
Each folder is tied to one sandbox by its own .p9m folder, so different folders can use different sandboxes, even on different Purgatorium servers. For another folder, do step 2 there: a new sandbox for it. The plugin needs no new setup.

To use a sandbox you already have, add its name: /p9m:init https://p9m.example.com k3x9q2. The page then asks for access to that sandbox (only one of your own), and it works the same way. This is how you move a folder to another sandbox, or connect a folder again after 90 days: Claude Code asks, then replaces the connection.

A new sandbox comes from Purgatorium's default template. For another one, name it: /p9m:init https://p9m.example.com --template <template>.

Used the earlier plugin, which asked for an address and a token? Run /plugin marketplace update p9m once, then /p9m:init in each project.

Installed the plugin when it was called p7y (/p7y:init)? Claude Code knows that one by its old name, and /plugin marketplace update p9m finds nothing. Remove it and add the new one, in a terminal, in the folder where you installed it:

claude plugin uninstall p7y@p7y --scope local
claude plugin marketplace remove p7y
claude plugin marketplace add p9m-team/p9m
claude plugin install p9m@p9m

--scope is where you installed it (claude plugin list shows it: user, project or local); a local one only from its own folder. Then start Claude Code again.

More details: Claude Code plugin.

docs.title: Share your app with your team on the Hub
docs.text:
The Hub is your team's showcase: a page at https://hub.<your Purgatorium domain> where colleagues find the apps you published, open them with one click, and vote for the ones they like. Colleagues who only use apps can sign in to the Hub alone.

What you need: an app already online in your sandbox (see Put your app online with Claude Code), and the Hub turned on in your Purgatorium (ask whoever runs it; it is HUB_ENABLED=true).

docs.title: 1. Publish
docs.text:
Tell your agent:

Publish the web app on the Hub, titled "Stock room", described as "Who took what from the stock room".

It adds labels to the app's service in its compose file and deploys again:

services:
  web:
    labels:
      p9m.publish: "true"
      p9m.title: "Stock room"
      p9m.description: "Who took what from the stock room"

Within about a minute and a half the app is on the Hub. In Purgatorium its App ports tab marks it On the Hub.

docs.title: 2. A picture on its card
docs.text:
Use /screenshot.png as its Hub image.

That adds p9m.image: "/screenshot.png": a picture the app itself serves (PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, up to 2 MB). Without it the Hub uses the page's own preview image, if it has one, or the title's first letter.

docs.title: 3. Share
docs.text:
Send colleagues the Hub's address. They see whether your app is running or asleep; Open wakes it if it sleeps. Everyone signed in can vote once for each app, yours too.

To take it off the Hub: remove the app from the Hub (the agent removes p9m.publish), or archive the sandbox.

All labels and settings: Hub.

docs.title: Put your app online with any agent
docs.text:
For Codex, Cursor, Claude Code without the plugin, or any agent that can run commands on your computer. Your project gets a small .p9m folder from Purgatorium; the agent uses it to build and run your app in your sandbox, and gives you its link.

What you need: the agent, Docker installed on your computer, and a Purgatorium account.

docs.title: 1. Get the .p9m folder
docs.text:
Users have no web UI in Purgatorium, so the folder comes one of two ways:

  • With Claude Code, once: in your app's folder, /p9m:init <address> makes you a sandbox and writes the .p9m folder. From then on any agent can use the folder; Claude Code is not needed any more.
  • From the admin: they open your sandbox in Purgatorium and download its zip (Let your agent deploy… → Download), p9m-<sandbox>.zip, and give it to you. Save it in your Downloads.

Either way it holds a token for this sandbox and its keys: treat it like a password. Do not email it or commit it.

docs.title: 2. Hand it to the agent
docs.text:
Open your app's folder with the agent and say:

Deploy this app to my p9m sandbox.

With a zip, say where it is: Set up the p9m zip from my Downloads in this project and deploy. The agent unpacks it into a .p9m folder in your project and deletes the zip. Then it builds your app in the sandbox, starts it and gives you its link. The .p9m folder keeps itself out of git on its own (it has its own .gitignore); leave it there, the agent uses it for every later update.

If the agent does not know what to do, point it to the instructions inside: read .p9m/README.md and deploy this app to my sandbox.

docs.title: 3. Update
docs.text: Changed something? Update the app in my sandbox. The same link shows the new version.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The folder's token expires in 90 days. Then run /p9m:init <address> <sandbox> in Claude Code again, or ask the admin for a new zip.
  • Lost the folder or the zip, or someone else got it? Tell the admin: they can make the old keys useless (Rotate Docker keys…) and revoke its token.
  • Sleep and wake work the same as with Claude Code: see Good to know there.

For agent builders: everything the agent does is in the agent guide.
